$VG KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VENTURE GLOBAL’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Venture Global’s call supports a selective investment framework rather than a broad bullish view on energy. The strongest positive implications accrue to suppliers with confirmed equipment exposure, gas producers and infrastructure owners positioned near expanding Gulf Coast demand, and LNG portfolio buyers gaining access to contractual supply. The clearest negative implication is for European gas-intensive production, where depleted storage and constrained global LNG availability threaten margins through winter and potentially into the 2027 replenishment season. The distinction between international LNG prices and domestic gas prices is critical: the current scarcity benefits businesses that monetize the geographic spread, while additional U.S. liquefaction and power demand can gradually increase domestic feedstock costs. Several relevant companies have already reported their quarterly results. Venture Global’s commentary primarily strengthens or challenges the durability of those outlooks rather than revealing previously unreported quarterly earnings.

POWER GENERATION, ELECTRICAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND LNG EQUIPMENT

BAKER HUGHES HAS CONFIRMED EXPOSURE ACROSS LIQUEFACTION, PIPELINE COMPRESSION AND PRIVATE POWER SYSTEMS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Baker Hughes (BKR: United States). Directional impact: positive. Magnitude: meaningful multiyear equipment and service opportunity, with moderate incremental visibility from this call rather than a newly disclosed earnings upgrade.

The supporting commentary is unusually specific. Venture Global discussed a 10 MTPA CP2 expansion incorporating 12 additional liquefaction trains, an initial Plaquemines expansion incorporating 8 trains, the Cloud Connector gas pipeline, and reservation agreements with Baker Hughes and GE Vernova for up to 16 power islands. Management also stated that the first power plants could be deployed into LNG expansions, providing an alternative use if data-center contracting takes longer than expected.

Baker Hughes’ own September announcement confirms an award for 13 turbine-driven gas compression systems for Cloud Connector and 8 liquefaction modules for the Plaquemines expansion. Its October power-framework announcement identifies additional scope in controls, electrical integration, E-houses and associated equipment. The economic exposure therefore extends beyond a generic association with rising LNG investment: Baker Hughes participates in moving the feed gas, liquefying it and supplying the integrated power architecture.

The most important implication is the diversification of the supplier’s revenue opportunity within the same customer relationship. An LNG expansion can generate compression and liquefaction demand even before the AI business is contracted. A subsequent data-center development can create additional power-equipment and integration demand without requiring a proportionate increase in LNG production. The ability to replicate an established architecture also supports execution efficiency and the development of an installed base requiring maintenance and services.

The near-term catalyst is conversion of the power framework into purchase orders. Baker Hughes’ announcement contemplated the first power-island order by year-end 2026, additional orders from 2027, and deliveries during 2028 to 2034. Orders, manufacturing milestones and any contractual progress payments can precede customer energization; the precise revenue-recognition profile is not disclosed.

The boundary is important: the September equipment awards and October framework predate this call. The call confirms project sequencing and customer commitment to development, but does not create 16 firm power-island orders. Neither Venture Global’s total project capital expenditure nor the full value of jointly supplied equipment can be attributed to Baker Hughes. The high-conviction positive is the breadth and duration of confirmed commercial exposure, not a quantifiable near-term EPS increase.

GE VERNOVA BENEFITS EVEN WHEN DATA CENTERS BYPASS THE PUBLIC GRID (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: GE Vernova (GEV: United States). Directional impact: positive. Magnitude: substantial strategic validation across Power and Electrification; the incremental financial contribution from this specific framework remains unquantified.

Venture Global identified agreements with GE Vernova and GE Grid Solutions for power islands and associated grid equipment. Management emphasized the scarcity of “near-term power generation equipment and the switchgear and transformers” and described an architecture incorporating generation, transformers, gas-insulated electrical equipment, batteries and additional layers of redundancy.

The important transmission mechanism is that avoiding the public grid does not eliminate electrical-infrastructure spending. It transfers much of that spending into a privately owned system. A grid-independent data center still requires generation, transformation, switching, protection, controls and contingency management. GE Vernova therefore retains exposure under both conventional utility-served development and the alternative island-mode architecture proposed by Venture Global.

The framework covers up to 16 units of approximately 720 MW each, equivalent to 11.52 GW of potential combined-cycle generation capacity. That is an indication of development scale, not contracted IT load or confirmed GE Vernova revenue. Gross generation capacity must accommodate auxiliary consumption, cooling, operating reserves and redundancy. The allocation of equipment value between suppliers is also undisclosed.

The call reinforces the durability of equipment demand when transmission interconnection becomes the bottleneck. It is consequently more supportive of generation and electrical-equipment suppliers than of the assumption that every announced AI project must create an equivalent regulated utility investment opportunity. Private power systems can bypass utility ownership while still purchasing substantial OEM content.

Near-term relevance is primarily order conversion and delivery-slot utilization. Longer-duration value comes from equipment execution and the associated service opportunity from 2028 onward. GE Vernova had already reported 122 GW of Gas Power equipment backlog and slot reservations on October 28 and expected at least 130 GW by year-end. The Venture Global framework must not simply be added to those figures: it may overlap existing reservations, and combined-cycle capacity is not necessarily measured on the same basis.

Management’s statement that equipment was secured at attractive prices also limits the inference that this particular customer agreement will realize unusually high OEM margins. The stronger conclusion is sustained demand and scarce manufacturing capacity, not proof of exceptional pricing on every reserved unit.

NITROGEN FERTILIZERS AND ENERGY-INTENSIVE INDUSTRY

YARA FACES A MATERIAL WINTER ENERGY-COST HEADWIND THAT HIGHER FERTILIZER PRICES MAY NOT FULLY OFFSET (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: Yara International (YAR: Norway). Directional impact: negative for European production margins and near-term earnings resilience. Magnitude: potentially material at group level, moderated by production flexibility, product pricing and non-European supply.

The call’s supporting evidence is management’s description of EU storage at its lowest early-November level since 2013 despite sharply higher LNG imports. Venture Global also highlighted reduced nuclear generation, weather-dependent wind output and the possibility that LNG prices remain elevated or increase further during winter. These conditions directly affect a European ammonia producer because natural gas is both a feedstock and a major energy input.

Yara’s own disclosures establish that this is an existing financial exposure rather than a theoretical sector association. Its Q3 EBITDA excluding special items declined to $675 million from $804 million, with higher European gas costs and lower deliveries outweighing higher product prices. Management explicitly identified accelerating European gas costs as a pressure on results.

The forward cost exposure is significant. Yara’s October presentation, using October 13 forward prices and approximately prior-year consumption volumes, illustrated European gas costs of about $860 million in Q4 2026 versus $430 million in Q4 2025, and $780 million in Q1 2027 versus $340 million in Q1 2026. Those comparisons imply approximately $430 million and $440 million of higher quarterly input costs before changes in product prices, actual production volumes and operating decisions. They are not forecasts of equivalent EBITDA declines.

Venture Global’s commentary strengthens the case that this cost pressure may persist beyond the winter demand peak. Low winter-ending inventories would increase European replenishment requirements during summer 2027. That extends the period in which European production economics depend on fertilizer prices compensating for expensive gas.

The near-term catalysts are European gas prices, winter weather, nitrate order pricing and production curtailment decisions. The October cost illustrations are already public and must not be treated as a fresh estimate reduction caused by this call. The new analytical value is confirmation from a major physical LNG supplier that the underlying scarcity conditions remain intact.

Yara’s global sourcing network, ability to substitute imported ammonia and prospective Gulf Coast Ammonia acquisition reduce the downside. The acquisition remained subject to closing conditions in its latest reviewed results, so its diversification benefits should not be treated as fully realized. The high-conviction conclusion is a material European conversion-margin headwind, not an assumption that every increase in gas costs passes directly through to consolidated earnings.

CF INDUSTRIES IS A RELATIVE BENEFICIARY OF THE INTERNATIONAL GAS SPREAD, NOT OF HIGHER GAS PRICES GENERALLY (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: CF Industries Holdings (CF: United States). Directional impact: positive relative to European nitrogen producers. Magnitude: meaningful support for operating margins and competitive position; incremental earnings depend on nitrogen pricing, production availability and North American gas costs.

The same call evidence that is negative for European ammonia production supports CF’s relative position: limited Middle Eastern LNG supply, depleted European storage and sustained competition for flexible cargoes. These developments raise the energy cost of marginal nitrogen production outside North America without necessarily causing an equivalent increase in CF’s domestic feedstock costs.

The earnings transmission operates through the global nitrogen cost curve. More expensive European gas compresses ammonia margins, encouraging curtailments or greater reliance on imports. Lower-cost North American producers can retain production and serve the resulting import requirement. The benefit can appear through stronger attainable product prices, more resilient utilization or protection of margins that would otherwise be competed away.

CF’s latest disclosures corroborate the mechanism. Its Q3 natural-gas cost in cost of sales, including realized derivatives, was $2.88/MMBtu, versus $2.96/MMBtu a year earlier. The company also reported that approximately 37% of European ammonia nameplate capacity was offline or operating at reduced rates in October. This is direct evidence that international gas-market stress is affecting competing production.

The most actionable distinction is between the level of global gas prices and the spread between international and North American gas costs. CF benefits from a wide spread, not from indiscriminate gas inflation. Venture Global’s expanding LNG production and proposed gas-fired AI capacity eventually create additional U.S. demand. If that raises Henry Hub materially without a corresponding increase in nitrogen prices, CF’s advantage narrows.

Near-term catalysts are winter gas-market conditions, European operating rates and purchasing for the 2027 agricultural season. CF had already released Q3 results on November 4, so Venture Global’s call reinforces the durability of the margin environment rather than forecasting an unreported quarterly beat.

The principal offsets are weaker fertilizer affordability, delayed purchasing, freight costs and CF’s own operational constraints, including its disclosed Yazoo City outage. European curtailments cannot be translated automatically into additional CF sales if its own capacity is unavailable. The preferred read-through is relative earnings resilience versus European production, rather than an unqualified forecast of higher absolute earnings.

NATURAL-GAS PRODUCTION AND MIDSTREAM INFRASTRUCTURE

COMSTOCK’S GEOGRAPHIC POSITION GAINS VALUE AS LNG AND COMPUTE COMPETE FOR GULF COAST GAS (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: Comstock Resources (CRK: United States). Directional impact: positive. Magnitude: potentially material over several years because of concentrated regional exposure and gas-price sensitivity; the immediate earnings effect is limited.

Venture Global specifically identified the Western Haynesville and Shelby Trough as sources of additional gas supply. Management described Cloud Connector extending toward Perryville and emphasized that upstream producers were achieving attractive results despite a relatively low-price environment. The call also maintained 2027 production guidance of 575 to 625 LNG cargoes, targeted July 2027 first LNG at CP2 and outlined a potential 5 GW compute development by 2031.

The transmission mechanism is physical demand and improved market access. Additional liquefaction increases gas consumption near the Gulf Coast. Pipelines connecting East Texas and North Louisiana production to coastal demand can improve basin realizations, reduce dependence on weaker regional outlets and support development of economically marginal drilling inventory. Gas-fired compute adds a separate demand source that is not dependent on LNG cargo prices once operating.

Comstock has direct geographic exposure, not a verified supply award to Venture Global. Its November results reported 122.4 Bcfe of quarterly production, up 9% year over year, including additional Western Haynesville wells. The relevant upside is stronger realized prices and a longer profitable development runway, rather than an entitlement to a specified share of Venture Global’s feed gas.

The power opportunity is large enough to matter physically but should not be accelerated into the near-term balance. Illustratively, 5 GW of continuous generation at a 7 MMBtu/MWh heat rate would consume approximately 0.8 Bcf/d. The first 250 MW increment would require only about 0.04 Bcf/d on the same assumptions. If the targets represent IT load, cooling and other overheads increase required generation. These are engineering sensitivities, not contracted gas demand.

The strongest near-term catalysts are CP2 construction milestones, gas-transport commitments and changes in regional forward prices. The larger fundamental effects occur from 2027 onward for LNG and from late 2028 onward for the proposed AI business.

Ownership and hedging constrain the equity sensitivity. Comstock’s announced SOCAR transaction would sell 20% of its interest in Legacy Haynesville upstream assets and 15% of its interest in Western Haynesville assets initially. Debt reduction improves financial resilience, but gross regional production growth cannot be attributed entirely to common shareholders. Likewise, stronger market prices only reach retained cash margins on production that is not already economically fixed through hedges.

WILLIAMS BENEFITS FROM GAS DELIVERABILITY AND VOLUME GROWTH EVEN IF LNG PRODUCER MARGINS NORMALIZE (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: The Williams Companies (WMB: United States). Directional impact: positive. Magnitude: moderate support for the existing growth platform and future contracting; no incremental Venture Global-specific earnings award is established.

Venture Global expects continued gas-basis pressure at Plaquemines, identified additional pipelines expected in 2028 and described Cloud Connector as necessary for LNG expansion, adjacent AI development and enhanced output from existing phases. This is evidence that the binding constraint is not simply the existence of U.S. gas reserves. It is the ability to deliver sufficient gas at the required location, pressure and reliability.

That supports the value of Williams’ Haynesville gathering and transmission platform. Its November results confirmed the completed Momentum Midstream acquisition and contributions from Louisiana Energy Gateway, which entered service in 2025. The company explicitly positioned those assets to serve growing LNG, power and industrial demand. This provides a verified operating connection to the regional demand theme without requiring an assumed ownership interest in Venture Global’s pipeline.

The important distinction from the LNG producer is margin exposure. Venture Global’s earnings per cargo can decline when commissioning volumes move onto lower-priced long-term contracts. The facility still consumes gas. For a fee-based gathering or transportation operator, sustained physical demand can support revenues even when the customer’s commodity-linked liquefaction margin normalizes.

The benefit is therefore stronger throughput, utilization, contract renewal and expansion economics, not a direct claim on elevated European LNG prices. Tight regional basis can encourage customers to sign longer-duration transport commitments, improving the financeability of additional infrastructure.

The near-term effect is primarily validation of growth already underway. Williams had reported Q3 results and discussed the acquired platform before Venture Global’s call. Existing reservation fees may already be earned irrespective of subsequent utilization, so higher throughput does not necessarily create a new fee stream. Incremental earnings require available capacity, volume-sensitive terms or new contracted investment.

Longer-duration catalysts are additional transportation agreements, expansion approvals and actual gas-demand commissioning. Cloud Connector itself should not be attributed to Williams, and the call does not establish that the 2 unnamed 2028 pipelines belong to Williams. The high-conviction read-through is favorable regional demand for its verified network, with only moderate confidence in additional financial upside beyond existing plans.

GLOBAL LNG PRODUCERS AND PORTFOLIO BUYERS

PLAQUEMINES COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS TRANSFER PROCUREMENT VALUE TO CONTRACT BUYERS (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies: Shell (SHEL: United Kingdom) and ConocoPhillips (COP: United States). Directional impact: positive for LNG procurement and portfolio flexibility. Magnitude: modest relative to each company’s consolidated earnings, but economically meaningful within the affected LNG portfolios.

Venture Global reported that Plaquemines Phase 1 reached commercial operations on October 31 and had loaded 6 cargoes for long-term customers. Thayer explicitly warned of an impact to Venture Global’s margins from commencement of those contracts. The company’s November 1 announcement identified Shell as the recipient of the first post-commercial-operation cargo.

This is a transfer of commercial value, not necessarily the creation of equivalent new physical supply. Much of the facility was already producing commissioning LNG. Commercial commencement changes the buyer’s access to contracted supply and the allocation of the margin between the LNG producer and customer.

For Shell, contractual access to U.S. LNG can reduce reliance on expensive replacement cargoes and improve optimization across shipping, destinations and downstream commitments. The economic gain depends on the difference between acquisition cost and the value of the cargo within Shell’s existing portfolio, after freight, hedging and customer obligations. It should not be measured by multiplying Venture Global’s residual $21/MMBtu to $22/MMBtu unsold-cargo assumption across Shell’s purchases.

The timing is near term: the relevant supply transition begins in Q4 2026 and continues into 2027. However, the first cargo was already announced before this earnings call. The call provides confirmation that deliveries are progressing, rather than revealing a previously unknown Shell contract.

ConocoPhillips represents the longer-duration version of the same portfolio strategy. Venture Global highlighted its new 1 MTPA agreement, and the October announcement specifies a 20-year purchase commitment starting in 2030. That provides future supply access without requiring ConocoPhillips to own the liquefaction facility. It is not a 2027 earnings catalyst or an equity investment in Venture Global.

For scale, each $1/MMBtu of retained margin on 1 MTPA corresponds to approximately $52 million annually before other costs. Actual contract economics are undisclosed, so that is a sensitivity rather than a forecast. The principal cross-portfolio insight is that lower reported margins at the LNG producer can coexist with better procurement economics for its customers.

CHENIERE’S MERCHANT EXPOSURE BENEFITS, BUT MOST OF THE 2026 UPGRADE IS ALREADY PUBLIC (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected company: Cheniere Energy (LNG: United States). Directional impact: positive for available marketing volumes and the durability of elevated international LNG margins. Magnitude: moderate incremental support for forward expectations, rather than a read-across of Venture Global’s 14% guidance increase.

Venture Global increased its 2026 EBITDA midpoint by $1.25 billion, raised its contracted-cargo coverage to approximately 99% and increased the weighted-average liquefaction fee on contracted cargoes to $6.46/MMBtu from $5.05/MMBtu. Management also argued that European storage shortfalls could sustain a favorable LNG market into 2027.

This supports the economic value of destination-flexible LNG and residual volumes that remain available for market-linked sales. Cheniere can benefit through its marketing activities and LNG not already economically fixed under long-term arrangements. Higher international prices do not create an equivalent margin increase on its entire production base, because much of that production is sold under contractual pricing structures and some commodity exposure is shared through upstream-linked arrangements.

Cheniere had already raised its own 2026 EBITDA guidance on October 29 to $8.75 billion to $9.25 billion from $7.90 billion to $8.40 billion. It also reported completion of the final Corpus Christi Stage 3 train in August. Venture Global’s results therefore corroborate a favorable physical market and monetization environment that Cheniere has already partly reflected in guidance.

The near-term trading relevance is principally the persistence of the winter scarcity premium and any further contracting of genuinely open volumes. It is not appropriate to apply Venture Global’s remaining-cargo fee assumption or sensitivity to Cheniere without matching open volumes, delivery periods and contractual economics.

The longer-duration implication is less uniformly positive. Venture Global’s targeted July 2027 CP2 startup, subsequent brownfield expansions and willingness to sign medium-term contracts add competing supply and procurement alternatives. Those developments are positive for Cheniere’s ability to operate within a growing LNG market, but can reduce scarcity margins on future uncontracted sales.

The high-conviction conclusion is positive for the earnings durability of currently available merchant LNG, with diminishing incremental 2026 exposure as cargoes are sold. It is not evidence that present scarcity margins should be capitalized indefinitely across Cheniere’s entire asset base.

text:
Texas Supreme Court Chief Justice-elect Maggie Ellis is drawing criticism from Christian religious liberty advocates after announcing plans to remove protections allowing judges to decline officiating same-sex weddings because of their sincerely held religious beliefs. Ellis, who became the first openly LGBTQ person elected to statewide office in Texas on November 3, said she wants to change the court's existing policy when she takes office in January 2027.

“One thing I'd like to do is work with the other justices to amend these orders to say either you perform all marriages, or none,” Ellis told The Dallas Morning News. She described the current exemption as “back-door discrimination.” The policy, adopted in October 2025, allows judges to decline wedding ceremonies that conflict with their religious convictions without violating judicial conduct rules.

Christian legal organization First Liberty Institute strongly opposed Ellis' proposal, warning that it could threaten religious freedom. President Kelly Shackelford emphasized that religious accommodation is a fundamental American right and pledged to defend affected judges. Although Ellis has announced her intentions, the current protections remain in place, and any change would require support from other members of the Texas Supreme Court.

text:
Is the $IREN thesis broken❓
The stock is down, analysts are cutting targets, rates are up, Texas flipped blue and Microsoft is delayed. The narrative writes itself: the $IREN thesis is broken.
The numbers say the opposite.

Payback is shrinking GPUs plus the data center now pay back in ~3 years, down from ~4.5 on the Microsoft contract a year ago. On a 5-year contract, that leaves two years of pure profit and a paid-off data center with 20+ years of life. The next contract in that shell only has to pay back the GPUs. IREN's latest GPU payback is ~18 months, which leaves roughly 42 of 60 months as profit, if we continue same prices after 5 years (very dpeculative)

Customers are funding the build: Microsoft prepaid 20% of contract value. IREN's latest contract prepays 90% of GPU cost, at 0% interest. Add ~50% debt on the GPUs and the whole project is funded without dilution or equity, with the data center still unlevered.

The dilution fear is overdone: IREN is ~$6B short of its $25–30B capex guide, but it sits on $12–15B of unlevered data centers and GPUs. Borrowing against that at ~10% would cover the rest of FY27. Future dilution looks very low, possibly zero.

Pricing keeps climbing Lease rates have gone from $10M to $22M/MW, short-term deals are signing at $40M/MW, and IREN's 4-year-old H100s just repriced +100%.

Higher rates matter less than you think: A $25M/MW contract at 24% interest is about as profitable as a $20M/MW contract at 9% (assuming 90% of GPU cost is debt and there's no prepayment). The pricing gains have already more than offset the rate move. Also, the rate being quoted is CoreWeave's corporate cost of debt, not asset-backed GPU financing. IREN just raised $400M in ABF at 9.5%, and that would be lower with IG backing.

Texas is a smaller risk than it looks: Hinojosa's proposal targets new permits. SW1 and SW2 already have approved grid connections and come online before 2028, and Republicans still hold the legislature. IREN builds miles from residents and doesn't push up local power bills, or use the local water. The real risk is a lower tax abatement (85% today), and IREN has ~35+ GW of pipeline beyond Texas.

The Microsoft delay is Microsoft's request: The delay comes from a cabling change Microsoft asked for, outside the original scope. Because IREN is fully integrated, it could make the change on short notice. The cost is 1–2 months, depending on equipment delivery. Horizon 1 was accepted. That says enough.

What the bears got right: The stock is down and price targets are being cut. For an investor, those are the things that matter least. Last year IREN went from $5 to $70 in six months on a sentiment shift alone. The same happened to the downside the last months. If GPU pricing collapse, the fundamentals will be hit hard.
But today I believe that the fundamentals have never been stronger. 
Stock price ≠ the company.

Im long, and strongly believe the stockprice will have a crazy repricing towards second half of 2027. (21$ today).

text:
$TSM / TSMC (TWSE: 2330) packed three outlook signals into Nov 10: a record October, a dividend hike from NT$7.0 to NT$9.0, and another US$40.9B of capacity approved by the board.

October revenue. NT$586.89B, up 14.7% MoM and 59.7% YoY. Jan–Oct: NT$4,485.62B, up 43.3% YoY. TSMC's own full-year 2026 guide is about 44% growth in US dollars.

Q4 pace (my math, one month only). The Q4 guide is US$52.3–54.3B at an assumed 31.8 NT$/US$, roughly NT$554–576B a month. October alone is about US$18.46B. Three months at that rate would be about US$55.4B, ~2% above the top of the guide. To reach the top end, November and December need only ~NT$570B a month, below what October already did.

The dividend. The board approved a NT$9.0 per share cash dividend for Q3 2026, up NT$2.0 (+28.6%) from NT$7.0 for each of Q1 and Q2. Total payout: NT$233.39B. Ex-dividend date March 11, 2027 for both common shares and ADSs; payment April 8, 2027. On Q3 EPS of NT$29.43, that's about 31% of the quarter's earnings. On the Oct 15 call, CFO Wendell Huang repeated the commitment to a "sustainable and steadily increasing cash dividend per share on both an annual and quarterly basis." This is that commitment in numbers.

The board. Capital appropriations of about US$40,926.70M for advanced-technology capacity; advanced packaging, mature and specialty capacity; fab construction and facility systems; and 2027 R&D capital, sustaining capex and capitalized leases. The August meeting approved US$29,442.50M. The board also approved up to US$500M to set up a strategic investment company for the semiconductor ecosystem, up to US$500M for Anthropic common shares at its IPO price, and up to US$500M for OpenAI Group PBC preferred stock.

What TSMC itself guided on Oct 15:
• Q4 gross margin 65–67%, operating margin 56.5–58.5%
• 2026 capex US$60–64B, reiterated; 2026–2028 capex "even more significantly higher" than the prior three years
• AI accelerator revenue CAGR of mid-to-high 50s% for 2024–2029; C.C. Wei: "it probably will be higher"
• N2 in volume production since 4Q25; N2-family annual capacity to more than double in 2027
• A14 risk production on track for 2027, volume production in 2028
• Nearly 20 fabs in progress: 13 leading-edge and advanced-packaging fabs in Taiwan, 5–6 overseas
• Arizona fab 2 volume production in 3Q27, slightly ahead of schedule; new Tainan N3 fabs in 1H27 and 1H28; Japan fab 2 on N3 in 2028

My read (inference): a higher dividend and a bigger capital budget on the same day say the cash engine funds both. In Q3, TSMC generated about NT$920B of operating cash flow against NT$443B of capex and NT$156B of dividends paid. A board doesn't lift the payout ~29% while approving US$40.9B more capacity unless it expects that capacity to fill.

Next markers: November revenue around Dec 10, then the January call, where TSMC typically sets its full-year outlook and capex budget.

["중선 털리면 트럼프 끝남 ㅋㅋㅋ" 비웃던 좌파들, 지금 남부 국경 보고 기절초풍한 이유]

2026년 중간선거 시즌 다가오니까 언론이랑 PC 진영 애들 신나서 축제 준비 들어갔던 거 다들 기억할 거다.

CNN이랑 뉴욕타임스가 매일같이 

"트럼프 국경 장벽 정책, 의회 권력 넘어가면 올스톱된다", 
"공화당 지지율 흔들려서 불법외국인 단속 동력 상실할 것"이라면서 설레발을 오지게 쳐댔지. 

멕시코 카르텔이랑 브로커 놈들도 "아싸 중선 끝나면 트럼프 힘 빠지니까 다시 국경 문 열린다, 물 들어올 때 노 젓자" 하면서 슬슬 루트 뚫을 각 재고 있었음. 

민주당 쪽에서는 "이제 인도주의적 개방이 돌아온다"며 입꼬리 씰룩거리고 있었고.

그런데 트럼프 이 영감이 중간선거 결과나 의회 눈치 보면서 사릴 인간이냐?

"아, 의회가 예산 깎고 법으로 태클 건다고? 그럼 법을 우회하면 그만이야~"

트럼프는 의회 표 계산 따위 개나 줘버리고, 국가안보 대통령 각서(NSPM-4) 딱 한 장 꺼내 들더니 남부 국경의 '루스벨트 보호구역' 연방 토지를 통째로 미 국방부(펜타곤)로 넘겨버렸음. 이름하여 '국방구역(National Defense Area, NDA)' 지정.

이게 무슨 미친 전략이냐면:
원래 미국에는 '포세 코미타투스(Posse Comitatus Act)'라는 빡센 법이 있어서 군대가 민간인을 함부로 체포하거나 국내 치안에 개입을 못 함. 

좌파 인권단체들이 맨날 "군대 동원은 위헌이다!"라며 법원 끌고 가던 단골 무기였지.

Jawar Mohammed, on 9 October you said you had long opposed Abiy Ahmed’s hostile rhetoric over sea access and would oppose any Eritrean incursion into Ethiopia.

 Days later, you outlined an advance on Assab and warned it could provoke resistance and outside intervention.

 By 28 October, you told AFP it was time to use military force to secure sea access. Now, in The Day After Isaias, you say port access “must not be imposed through military force.” Which of your October positions are you asking readers to forget?

Reuters described you as a former ally who helped bring Abiy to power. You became a prominent opponent, were detained in 2020 and were still publicly criticising his government in late 2024. Now you ask Eritreans to trust his army to cross their border, help oversee a transition and leave their sovereignty intact. Eritreans are entitled to scrutinise the power you would have Abiy exercise in their country.

Your reading of the Horn is amateurish. You list risks in Tigray, Sudan and the Red Sea, then write as though Addis Ababa could manage them once its troops cross the border. You already conceded that Eritreans who oppose Isaias could resist a prolonged Ethiopian military presence.

 The G7 warned on 11 November that a wider war could endanger regional security, humanitarian operations and Red Sea trade. You have drawn two routes on a map. You have yet to explain why the region would follow either script.

The same rule applies in both directions. Any proven Eritrean incursion deserves condemnation. Asmara denied the reported October incursion, which Reuters could not verify independently. Even if an armed attack is established, self-defence under Article 51 must be necessary and proportionate.

 A border attack gives Ethiopia no licence to seize Assab for leverage or impose a government in Asmara. If Ethiopian forces exercise effective control over Eritrean territory without consent, the law of occupation applies, however brief the deployment.

You call Isaias an Egyptian proxy. Cairo and Asmara acknowledge cooperation, but you offer no evidence that Cairo directs Eritrean policy. In contrast Abiy is a known UAE proxy and responsible for the suffering of the Sudanese people, but it looks like accountability is on sight.

You say Ethiopia’s latest Tigray campaigns were viewed more favourably. By whom?The ENDF has committed unspeakable crimes across Tigray, Amhara and other parts of Ethiopia. Human Rights Watch also documented arbitrary detention and deportation of Eritrean refugees by Ethiopian security forces. That record belongs in any serious assessment of civilian protection.

Your refugee figures broadly check out. UNHCR recorded 181,264 Eritrean refugees in Ethiopia at the end of 2020 and 117,472 Eritrean refugees and asylum seekers on 31 October 2026.  Eritreans have every right to criticise their  government if any, but  they also have the right to decide who governs them.

You tell the story of Harnet, who understood what Eritrean independence meant without ever setting foot in the country. Take her seriously. Eritrea joined the UN in 1993. In 2018, both governments agreed to resume transport and trade links. Ethiopia could negotiate port access before your call for military action, and it can do so today. If your respect for Eritrean sovereignty begins after Ethiopian troops have crossed the border and reshaped the government, you have already decided how much sovereignty Eritreans get to exercise.

text:
BRING BACK JUCO FOOTBALL TO ARIZONA!

This one is personal to me.

Before I played football at BYU, I played junior college football in Arizona at Eastern Arizona College (under Kalani Sitake, his first coaching gig) and Glendale Community College.

Those programs gave young men like me an opportunity to develop physically, mentally, academically and athletically. They gave us structure, discipline, accountability and a pathway to four-year universities.

For whatever reason, Arizona decided to eliminate junior college football a few years ago, effectively dismantling the Western States Football League (WSFL).

I believe that was a mistake.

Jim Harbaugh once described football as one of the last bastions of toughness for young men. I couldn’t agree more.

Young men need purpose. They need structure. They need accountability. They need teams. They need coaches who challenge them, believe in them and hold them to a higher standard.

Football provides all of those things.

Now there’s some encouraging news coming out of Arizona.

I’ve been receiving updates from Joe Kersting, former head football coach at Glendale Community College, regarding efforts to restore JUCO football.

Here’s where things stand:

The Maricopa Community College District Governing Board has directed Chancellor Dr. Steven Bloomberg to evaluate the financial feasibility of bringing football back.

According to Kersting, Bloomberg is committed to restoring football and wants to develop a process for moving forward.

John David Crow, Ryan Caraciollo and Susan Winder helped bring significant public attention to the issue through their campaigns. Their videos reportedly generated more than 2 million views.
The initial focus is restoring football at Mesa, Phoenix, Scottsdale and Glendale Community Colleges.

If Maricopa develops a sustainable model, there’s optimism that Eastern Arizona, Arizona Western and Pima could eventually bring their programs back as well.

That’s potentially seven Arizona junior college football programs.

Look, I understand the financial challenges. Football isn’t inexpensive. Equipment, insurance, travel, facilities, coaching and operational expenses all add up.

But eliminating opportunities for hundreds of young men shouldn’t be the answer.

We need to figure out a cost-effective, sustainable way to bring these programs back. Whether that’s through private funding, corporate sponsorships, community partnerships, shared resources or a restructured conference model, there has to be a serious conversation about what’s possible.

Not every young man is ready for Division I football at 18 years old. Some need another year or two to mature, develop academically, get stronger and earn their opportunity.

I was one of those young men.

JUCO football helped shape the trajectory of my life, and I know countless others who can say the same.

This is bigger than football. It’s about education, opportunity, mentorship and helping young men become productive members of society.

I appreciate Joe Kersting, John David Crow, Ryan Caraciollo and everyone else who continues fighting to restore these opportunities.

Gotta  find a way to make the numbers work.

The U.S. is now scrambling to secure its own supply.

One of the most important lessons of the last few years is the importance of securing sovereignty over your own supply of energy and materials.

Global supply chains have proved far more fragile than anyone assumed. They are exposed to foreign leverage, and that exposure becomes acute in times of war and conflict, or in a strategic contest like the current race for AI.

Both of which are underway and show no signs of slowing down.

That race will be decided less by talent or code than it will by physical inputs: the power to run it and the materials to build it. Copper is foundational to both, and Washington now treats it as a matter of national security.

And events from last week are evidence of that.

Freeport committed $4.5B to expand its Bagdad mine in Arizona. The expansion more than doubles the mine's copper output and makes it the second-largest copper mine in the country. That said, the first new copper is not expected until mid-2030.

The next day, Rio Tinto put $144M into Resolution Copper, a deposit that could eventually meet up to 25% of U.S. demand. It is also not expected to produce until the mid-2030s.

This is not private ambition acting alone. Washington is fast-tracking permits, tariffing imports and clearing federal land to bring this supply home.

JPMorgan sees U.S. output more than doubling over time, but places most of that growth after 2030. The scale of today's decline puts this in context, and I've spoken about it in many posts over the last few weeks.

In 1900 the U.S. produced roughly half of the world's copper.

Today it produces less than 5%, and it relies on imports for 57% of the refined copper it consumes.

New mines take a decade or more to bring into production, while demand from power grids, data centres and electrification is arriving now.

Sovereignty in this sense does not stop at the national border. It extends to North American companies developing resources in friendly jurisdictions across the Americas.

Chile is the world's largest copper producer. Peru ranks among the top three, and last week its economy minister said the country could double its copper output within 5 to 10 years. Both have long-standing free trade agreements with the U.S.

That is precisely where we ( $COPR ) are operating, exploring for copper and gold at Sombrero in Peru.

The deposits discovered today are what will close that gap over the next decade.

Jacob Soboroff: “ok, let's talk about a potentially major, i'm talking about like mega, side effect of these midterm elections. the electoral college has been a fixture of american presidential elections since the country's founding. but after this week's midterms, the system that determines who becomes president of the united states could be closer than ever to a major overhaul. here's how it works. when americans vote for president, they are technically voting for a slate of electors that are pledged to their preferred candidate. forgive me if you know this already. each state gets a certain number of electoral votes based on its representation in congress. there are 538 in total, and a candidate needs to get at least 270 to win the presidency. in nearly every state, it's winner take all. maine and nebraska are the exceptions. they allocate some electoral votes by congressional districts. so, even if a candidate wins the popular vote nationally, like they get the most votes, they can still lose the election if they do not win enough electoral votes. but what if i told you that with the results of this year's midterms, the electoral college could effectively be bypassed without amending the constitution? democrats now have an opportunity to advance something called the national popular vote interstate compact. states can choose to opt into the compact. this is how it works. those states commit their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the popular vote, regardless of who wins their individual state. it was launched in 2006. eighteen states and washington, d.c. already have adopted the compact. but the agreement takes effect only when it is signed by enough states that represent a majority of the electoral college, at least 270 electoral votes. right now, it's pretty close. the states that are signed on account for 222. but tuesday's democratic sweep could put that number within reach. pennsylvania, michigan, wisconsin, nevada, arizona, democrats won control of the governor's offices and both statehouse chambers. there are five states. those five states together hold 61 electoral votes. if all five of them join the compact, that brings the total electoral votes to, drum roll, please, 283. that is 13 more than what is needed. that would mean that the winner of the national popular vote could effectively become president in 2028. but there's still a catch. lawmakers in those states have to pass the legislation, and there could be legal challenges. so for now, the electoral college is not going anywhere. but after this week's midterms, the rules for electing america's next president could be up for fundamental change. joining me now is akhil amar, professor of law and political science at yale law school. he is the author of born equal, remaking america's constitution. it's great to see you.”

Akhil Amar: “nice to see you. thanks for having me, jacob.”

Jacob Soboroff: “thank you so much. did i get that right?”

Akhil Amar: “yes, you did. one thing i could perhaps add is that i'm one of the co-inventors of this idea, and i'm not sure it's actually, in its current incarnation, a great idea. so this is a good moment for us to actually have a national conversation about the thing. one analogy might be it's like ai, wow, it can make our life better. i use it all the time as a search engine, but if it's got some glitches in the chip, it could melt down the universe. and this one, in its current incarnation, and remember, i'm one of the co-inventors of it, i may have some glitches in the chip.”

Jacob Soboroff: “tell me why. tell me more.”

Akhil Amar: “okay. so in 2000, of course, people all remember that george w. bush won the electoral college even though al gore got more votes. that didn't sit right with me. i happen to be a democrat, but i also just believe in one person, one vote. a year later, i posted something on the internet. it was a version of the national popular interstate compact, but it had some different features than the one that many states have adopted. so first, in my vision, i wanted it to be a bipartisan reform. yeah, the electoral college favored george w. bush in 2000, but it could have favored al gore. in fact, i was on msnbc, a precursor to ms now, actually saying on election day as possible, al gore will win the electoral college with george w. bush getting a popular vote majority. but as voted on by the various states thus far, we haven't gotten a lot of buy-in from republican states, and that's not a good sign for our country if one side thinks it's a partisan scheme to help the other. we could modify that if we just had a phase-in, a sunrise rule saying, oh, it won't go into effect for a few years, but that's one thing. but now here are some other bigger glitches. the big idea behind it is one person, one vote, uniformity, we should all be equal. that's how we pick governors in every state. but the problem is, without a lot of central oversight, we're not going to get full equality because different states let people vote in different ways. suppose california says, we're going to let 17-year-olds vote because we want more californians voting in this system, and texas says, well, we want 16-year-olds to vote, and arkansas says, well, we want dogs to vote or parents to vote for children.”

Jacob Soboroff: “oh my goodness.”

Akhil Amar: “so you're going to need a lot of oversight there. suppose some states actually say, we didn't like this system. we didn't buy into it. the election wasn't close in our state. it's close nationally. we need a recount, but we're not going to participate in a national recount. so there are other glitches as well.”

Jacob Soboroff: “wasn't that sort of the criticism, though, of this gerrymandering effort, that this was going to be sort of political open war by going back and forth, and gavin newsom called it fighting fire with fire, but he determined that democrats had to do this in order to make sure that the will of the people was heard. i guess what i'm hearing you say now is, yeah, the nature of the system, the un-united states of america when it comes to the ways and the days on which we vote, could be part of the problem here, making it unequal in selecting people using the national popular vote. but wasn't that the intention in the first place that the states and the localities are supposed to come up with the time, place, and manner of how we do this?”

Akhil Amar: “well, originally, the electoral college has some really troubling roots. it was, in part, accommodating a slavery system in the south, giving them extra electoral votes for their slaves, the three-fifths compromise. but if the idea is equality, we're going to need, actually, a kind of a uniform system of administration. and here's another concern. do you want donald trump or any incumbent president in charge of that system? states do it pretty well. we picked governors, one person, one vote statewide, but governors don't typically control their state attorneys general, their state secretaries of state who are independently elected. so when donald trump tried to pressure raffenberger and kemp back in 2000 in georgia, even though they were members of his party, they resisted. but in a proper national popular vote, interstate compact system, where you're going to need more uniformity, actually, do you want him being able to call all the shots to have federal monitors in every state and locality? let's think about that. also, i'm a democrat, and i didn't design this as a partisan scheme. but truthfully, going forward, now that texas is at a minimum in play, maybe even leaning toward us if we don't screw up, we democrats and ohio and north carolina and arizona and oh my god, georgia, democrats and republicans cannot win the presidency under the old rules without texas. it's almost impossible. definitely. they need texas or ohio. and so, you know, to the extent that some of my democratic friends voted for this thing because they thought it would help democrats, remember, i'm a democrat, but i didn't devise this as a partisan system. i actually think this could backfire big time. there could be chaos. state supreme courts could say under our state constitution, it has to be the people of this state that make the decision. so all i'm saying is this is a moment to kind of go slow, carefully consider this. and and we can actually have a great national conversation about the electoral college, which is deeply flawed, has tainted roots in american slavery, but also has some virtues, one of which is it's decentralized and very hard for people in the center to basically manipulate and corrupt. and we just saw that in the last election.”

Jacob Soboroff: “wow. this is going to be a fascinating, fascinating national conversation around this. a lot of things that i hadn't i hadn't considered yet. i'm so glad.”

Akhil Amar: “go ahead.”

Jacob Soboroff: “real quick. we've got to run.”

Akhil Amar: “yeah. i have a free weekly podcast. we're going to talk about these issues this week. it's called the marcus constitution. feel free to tune in.”

Jacob Soboroff: “all right. akhil amar, a constitutional law scholar and professor of law and political science at yale law school. thank you again.”

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

In an industry in constant flux, sticking your neck out to predict what’s coming next may seem reckless. (AI bubble? What AI bubble?) But for the last few years we’ve done just that—and we’re doing it again. 

How did we do last time? We picked five hot AI trends to look out for in 2025, including what we called generative virtual playgrounds, a.k.a world models (check: From Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 to World Labs’s Marble, tech that can generate realistic virtual environments on the fly keeps getting better and better); so-called reasoning models (check: Need we say more? Reasoning models have fast become the new paradigm for best-in-class problem solving); a boom in AI for science (check: OpenAI is now following Google DeepMind by setting up a dedicated team to focus on just that); AI companies that are cozier with national security (check: OpenAI reversed position on the use of its technology for warfare to sign a deal with the defense-tech startup Anduril to help it take down battlefield drones); and legitimate competition for Nvidia (check, kind of: China is going all in on developing advanced AI chips, but Nvidia’s dominance still looks unassailable—for now at least). 

So what’s coming in 2026? Here are our big bets for the next 12 months. 

More Silicon Valley products will be built on Chinese LLMs

The last year shaped up as a big one for Chinese open-source models. In January, DeepSeek released R1, its open-source reasoning model, and shocked the world with what a relatively small firm in China could do with limited resources. By the end of the year, “DeepSeek moment” had become a phrase frequently tossed around by AI entrepreneurs, observers, and builders—an aspirational benchmark of sorts. 

It was the first time many people realized they could get a taste of top-tier AI performance without going through OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.

Open-weight models like R1 allow anyone to download a model and run it on their own hardware. They are also more customizable, letting teams tweak models through techniques like distillation and pruning. This stands in stark contrast to the “closed” models released by major American firms, where core capabilities remain proprietary and access is often expensive.

As a result, Chinese models have become an easy choice. Reports by CNBC and Bloomberg suggest that startups in the US have increasingly recognized and embraced what they can offer.

One popular group of models is Qwen, created by Alibaba, the company behind China’s largest e-commerce platform, Taobao. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct alone has 8.85 million downloads, making it one of the most widely used pretrained LLMs. The Qwen family spans a wide range of model sizes alongside specialized versions tuned for math, coding, vision, and instruction-following, a breadth that has helped it become an open-source powerhouse.

Other Chinese AI firms that were previously unsure about committing to open source are following DeepSeek’s playbook. Standouts include Zhipu’s GLM and Moonshot’s Kimi. The competition has also pushed American firms to open up, at least in part. In August, OpenAI released its first open-source model. In November, the Allen Institute for AI, a Seattle-based nonprofit, released its latest open-source model, Olmo 3. 

Even amid growing US-China antagonism, Chinese AI firms’ near-unanimous embrace of open source has earned them goodwill in the global AI community and a long-term trust advantage. In 2026, expect more Silicon Valley apps to quietly ship on top of Chinese open models, and look for the lag between Chinese releases and the Western frontier to keep shrinking—from months to weeks, and sometimes less.

—Caiwei Chen

The US will face another year of regulatory tug-of-war

T​​he battle over regulating artificial intelligence is heading for a showdown. On December 11, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aiming to neuter state AI laws, a move meant to handcuff states from keeping the growing industry in check. In 2026, expect more political warfare. The White House and states will spar over who gets to govern the booming technology, while AI companies wage a fierce lobbying campaign to crush regulations, armed with the narrative that a patchwork of state laws will smother innovation and hobble the US in the AI arms race against China.

Under Trump’s executive order, states may fear being sued or starved federal funding if they clash with his vision for light-touch regulation. Big Democratic states like California—which just enacted the nation’s first frontier AI law requiring companies to publish safety testing for their AI models—will take the fight to court, arguing that only Congress can override state laws. But states that can’t afford to lose federal funding, or fear getting in Trump’s crosshairs, might fold. Still, expect to see more state lawmaking on hot-button issues, especially where Trump’s order gives states a green light to legislate. With chatbots accused of triggering teen suicides and data centers sucking up more and more energy, states will face mounting public pressure to push for guardrails. 

In place of state laws, Trump promises to work with Congress to establish a federal AI law. Don’t count on it. Congress failed to pass a moratorium on state legislation twice in 2025, and we aren’t holding out hope that it will deliver its own bill this year. 

AI companies like OpenAI and Meta will continue to deploy powerful super-PACs to support political candidates who back their agenda and target those who stand in their way. On the other side, super-PACs supporting AI regulation will build their own war chests to counter. Watch them duke it out at next year’s midterm elections.

The further AI advances, the more people will fight to steer its course, and 2026 will be another year of regulatory tug-of-war—with no end in sight.

—Michelle Kim

Chatbots will change the way we shop

Imagine a world in which you have a personal shopper at your disposal 24-7—an expert who can instantly recommend a gift for even the trickiest-to-buy-for friend or relative, or trawl the web to draw up a list of the best bookcases available within your tight budget. Better yet, they can analyze a kitchen appliance’s strengths and weaknesses, compare it with its seemingly identical competition, and find you the best deal. Then once you’re happy with their suggestion, they’ll take care of the purchasing and delivery details too.

But this ultra-knowledgeable shopper isn’t a clued-up human at all—it’s a chatbot. This is no distant prediction, either. Salesforce recently said it anticipates that AI will drive $263 billion in online purchases this holiday season. That’s some 21% of all orders. And experts are betting on AI-enhanced shopping becoming even bigger business within the next few years. By 2030, between $3 trillion and $5 trillion annually will be made from agentic commerce, according to research from the consulting firm McKinsey. 

Unsurprisingly, AI companies are already heavily invested in making purchasing through their platforms as frictionless as possible. Google’s Gemini app can now tap into the company’s powerful Shopping Graph data set of products and sellers, and can even use its agentic technology to call stores on your behalf. Meanwhile, back in November, OpenAI announced a ChatGPT shopping feature capable of rapidly compiling buyer’s guides, and the company has struck deals with Walmart, Target, and Etsy to allow shoppers to buy products directly within chatbot interactions. 

Expect plenty more of these kinds of deals to be struck within the next year as consumer time spent chatting with AI keeps on rising, and web traffic from search engines and social media continues to plummet. 

—Rhiannon Williams

An LLM will make an important new discovery

I’m going to hedge here, right out of the gate. It’s no secret that large language models spit out a lot of nonsense. Unless it’s with monkeys-and-typewriters luck, LLMs won’t discover anything by themselves. But LLMs do still have the potential to extend the bounds of human knowledge.

We got a glimpse of how this could work in May, when Google DeepMind revealed AlphaEvolve, a system that used the firm’s Gemini LLM to come up with new algorithms for solving unsolved problems. The breakthrough was to combine Gemini with an evolutionary algorithm that checked its suggestions, picked the best ones, and fed them back into the LLM to make them even better.

Google DeepMind used AlphaEvolve to come up with more efficient ways to manage power consumption by data centers and Google’s TPU chips. Those discoveries are significant but not game-changing. Yet. Researchers at Google DeepMind are now pushing their approach to see how far it will go.

And others have been quick to follow their lead. A week after AlphaEvolve came out, Asankhaya Sharma, an AI engineer in Singapore, shared OpenEvolve, an open-source version of Google DeepMind’s tool. In September, the Japanese firm Sakana AI released a version of the software called SinkaEvolve. And in November, a team of US and Chinese researchers revealed AlphaResearch, which they claim improves on one of AlphaEvolve’s already better-than-human math solutions.

There are alternative approaches too. For example, researchers at the University of Colorado Denver are trying to make LLMs more inventive by tweaking the way so-called reasoning models work. They have drawn on what cognitive scientists know about creative thinking in humans to push reasoning models toward solutions that are more outside the box than their typical safe-bet suggestions.

Hundreds of companies are spending billions of dollars looking for ways to get AI to crack unsolved math problems, speed up computers, and come up with new drugs and materials. Now that AlphaEvolve has shown what’s possible with LLMs, expect activity on this front to ramp up fast.    

—Will Douglas Heaven

Legal fights heat up

For a while, lawsuits against AI companies were pretty predictable: Rights holders like authors or musicians would sue companies that trained AI models on their work, and the courts generally found in favor of the tech giants. AI’s upcoming legal battles will be far messier.

The fights center on thorny, unresolved questions: Can AI companies be held liable for what their chatbots encourage people to do, as when they help teens plan suicides? If a chatbot spreads patently false information about you, can its creator be sued for defamation? If companies lose these cases, will insurers shun AI companies as clients?

In 2026, we’ll start to see the answers to these questions, in part because some notable cases will go to trial (the family of a teen who died by suicide will bring OpenAI to court in November).

At the same time, the legal landscape will be further complicated by President Trump’s executive order from December—see Michelle’s item above for more details on the brewing regulatory storm.

No matter what, we’ll see a dizzying array of lawsuits in all directions (not to mention some judges even turning to AI amid the deluge).

—James O’Donnell
