text:
AI – Protectionism and the New Geography of Global Trade 
Principal judgment: Artificial intelligence is not reversing protectionism. It is creating an increasingly important exception to it, as governments confront the economic costs of restricting access to the technologies, intermediate goods and international production networks required for AI development.

The evidence establishes a striking divergence between political restrictions on trade and the continued expansion of international commerce. In its October 2026 outlook, the World Trade Organization (WTO) raised its forecast for world merchandise trade volume growth to 3.9% in 2026, compared with 1.9% forecast in March. AI-enabling goods accounted for 47% of the year-on-year increase in global merchandise trade value during the first half of 2026, while trade in those goods expanded by 67%. Global Trade Outlook and Statistics — WTO — Oct 2026

This expansion is occurring alongside an intensification of restrictive trade policy. According to the WTO–IMF Trade Policy Activity Index, average global trade-policy activity in January–May 2026 was nearly twice its 2024 level, with restrictive measures driving much of the increase. Updated WTO-IMF TPA Index Shows Continued Rise in Global Trade Policy Activity — WTO — Jul 2026

The result is not a return to unrestricted globalisation, but an emerging system of selective economic openness: governments seek domestic industrial capabilities while remaining dependent on foreign components, specialised production, investment, services and technological expertise.

The greatest strategic vulnerability is concentration. The ten largest trading economies in AI-enabling goods accounted for approximately 85% of global exports and 80% of global imports in 2025. Expansion therefore coexists with substantial exposure to supply disruptions and geopolitical restrictions.

For policymakers, the central challenge is to reconcile technological security, national industrial capacity and internationally competitive access to AI infrastructure. The decisive uncertainty is whether AI-led trade growth becomes a durable, broad-based productivity transformation or remains dependent on a concentrated investment cycle vulnerable to financial repricing and political intervention.

AI Is Making Protectionism More Expensive — Without Making Governments Free Traders
Artificial intelligence is accelerating global commerce while concentrating technological power, financial exposure and industrial dependence. The result is not a return to free trade, but a more selective and politically controlled globalisation.

Artificial intelligence is exposing the central contradiction of contemporary industrial policy: governments seeking technological sovereignty increasingly depend on the international production networks they are trying to control. The World Trade Organization forecasts 3.9% growth in merchandise trade volume in 2026, even as restrictive trade-policy activity has intensified. AI-enabling goods accounted for 47% of the increase in global merchandise trade value during the first half of 2026. Washington restricts strategic technology exports while financing domestic semiconductor production; Beijing mobilises public capital to reduce foreign dependence; Brussels subsidises manufacturing while negotiating digital market access. The immediate stakes extend beyond trade balances. Industrial competitiveness, public finances, energy infrastructure and national security increasingly depend on whether governments can distinguish dependencies worth reducing from international relationships they cannot economically afford to dismantle.

Protectionism Is Rising, but Technology Is Pulling Trade in the Opposite Direction
The WTO–IMF Trade Policy Activity Index recorded restrictive intervention during January–May 2026 at nearly twice its 2024 average and approximately one-quarter above its 2025 level. Yet the WTO revised its forecast for 2026 merchandise trade volume growth from 1.9% in March to 3.9% in October, with a further 4.1% projected for 2027.

This divergence does not demonstrate that tariffs are ineffective. It demonstrates that trade restrictions and commercial demand operate through different mechanisms. Governments can raise barriers against selected suppliers while companies increase purchases of indispensable intermediate goods, redirect procurement or reorganise production across jurisdictions. Trade volumes can survive this adjustment even as transaction costs increase.

The distinction between value and volume is critical. During the first half of 2026, global merchandise trade increased 15% in current-dollar value but only 3.5% in volume. Higher prices for fuels and electronic components contributed to the difference. The nominal expansion of commerce therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to higher physical production or productivity.

The strongest conclusion from the WTO data is narrower but more consequential: the international economy is becoming more interventionist without becoming uniformly less interconnected. Artificial intelligence is a principal reason that this distinction now matters.

The Numbers Reveal a Concentrated Investment Cycle, Not a Universal Trade Revival
Trade in AI-enabling goods increased 16% in 2024, 31% in 2025 and 67% year-on-year during the first half of 2026. Their share of world merchandise trade value reached 14.8%, compared with approximately 7–8% during 2016–2023.

The scale of this expansion creates an important asymmetry. AI-related hardware accounted for almost half of the increase in world merchandise trade value during the first six months of 2026, but production and demand remain concentrated. The WTO estimates that the ten leading economies accounted for approximately 85% of AI-enabling goods exports and 80% of imports in 2025.

Global trade can consequently accelerate while industrial power becomes more concentrated. A rising number of international transactions does not necessarily mean that additional countries control the technologies required to produce the goods being traded.

The International Energy Agency provides the corresponding investment evidence. Capital expenditure by five major technology companies exceeded US$400 billion in 2025, with a further increase of approximately 75% anticipated in 2026. This expenditure supports demand for processors, memory, servers, networking equipment and electricity infrastructure.

The WTO’s trade outlook and the IEA’s investment assessment therefore describe related stages of the same economic process: expectations of future AI demand generate present capital expenditure, which creates international equipment orders before the anticipated productivity gains necessarily materialise.

The central vulnerability is that investment is measurable immediately; its economic return is not.

Semiconductor Sovereignty Breaks Down at the Weakest Production Stage
The industrial structure supporting AI makes comprehensive technological self-sufficiency exceptionally difficult.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reported NT$3.809 trillion in 2025 revenue, with advanced process technologies accounting for 74% of wafer revenue. Customers headquartered in North America represented 75% of the company’s revenue, demonstrating the geographical separation between commercial demand and manufacturing capabilities.

The Netherlands occupies a different position. ASML reported €32.7 billion in 2025 sales, including deliveries of 48 extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems and 279 deep-ultraviolet systems. Its importance derives from specialised manufacturing equipment rather than the domestic production of finished AI processors.

Advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory introduce additional dependencies. A processor cannot deliver its intended performance merely because sufficient logic-chip fabrication capacity exists. Memory bandwidth, component integration, manufacturing qualification and packaging capacity must also be available.

The United States has attempted to address selected vulnerabilities through domestic investment incentives. The November 2024 federal award for TSMC Arizona provided for up to US$6.6 billion in direct funding and US$5 billion in potential loans, associated with a manufacturing programme exceeding US$65 billion. These are funding arrangements and investment plans, not interchangeable measures of expenditure already disbursed or operational production.

The same distinction applies to electricity. The IEA estimates global data-centre electricity consumption at 485 TWh in 2025, potentially reaching approximately 950 TWh by 2030. Manufacturing access to advanced processors becomes economically insufficient when grid connections, transformers, cooling systems or electricity availability constrain their deployment.

Technological sovereignty is therefore not established by announcing a semiconductor factory or financing a data centre. It depends on the operational availability of an entire system of complementary capabilities.

Washington and Beijing Are Managing Access, Not Ending Interdependence
The United States has developed an increasingly differentiated export-control regime. In December 2024, the Bureau of Industry and Security introduced restrictions involving 24 semiconductor manufacturing-equipment categories, three software categories, high-bandwidth memory and 140 additions to the Entity List.

Yet on 15 January 2026, the Department of Commerce introduced case-by-case licensing treatment for specified advanced computing products exported to China and Macau, including the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X, subject to technical and compliance conditions.

The adjustment is revealing. Washington did not abandon export controls. It established a narrower channel for commercial transactions while preserving government authority over eligibility, performance thresholds and recipients.

China’s response has emphasised domestic industrial capability. The third phase of its National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund was established in May 2024 with approximately RMB 344 billion in registered capital. The amount demonstrates financing ambition, not completed manufacturing capacity.

Both governments are therefore pursuing forms of selective industrial sovereignty: the United States through technological access controls and domestic production incentives; China through capital mobilisation and efforts to develop substitute capabilities.

The resulting competition affects third countries whose companies supply equipment, materials, memory and manufacturing services to both markets. Restrictions can redirect investment and production without eliminating upstream dependence. Relocating final assembly does not necessarily change the origin of the equipment, intellectual property or specialised components on which production relies.

The emerging divide is not between economies that trade and economies that do not. It is between technologies permitted to circulate and capabilities governments increasingly seek to control.

Europe and India Are Spending on Sovereignty, but Not on the Same Technologies
Europe’s industrial response illustrates the fiscal and technological complexity of semiconductor sovereignty.

The European Commission associates the original European Chips Act with more than €52 billion in mobilised public and private investment. Its June 2026 Chips Act 2.0 proposal extends the policy discussion towards industrial demand, supply resilience and the relationship between manufacturing and the broader technology system.

National projects demonstrate why aggregate European figures conceal substantial differences.

Italy authorised approximately €2 billion in state aid for STMicroelectronics’ Catania silicon-carbide programme, associated with a project of approximately €5 billion. Full capacity is expected in 2032. The investment targets power-semiconductor capabilities rather than the most advanced AI logic processors.

France supported the STMicroelectronics–GlobalFoundries Crolles programme, involving approximately €7.5 billion in investment and up to €2.9 billion in public assistance.

Germany obtained European Commission approval in August 2024 for €5 billion in state aid supporting the European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company project in Dresden. Its planned 28/22-nanometre and 16/12-nanometre production targets industrial and automotive requirements, with full capacity planned for 2029.

These investments are not technologically equivalent. Their economic justification depends on the specific components required by downstream industries, not on their contribution to an undifferentiated national semiconductor-production total.

The United Kingdom has adopted a more specialised approach. Its National Semiconductor Strategy committed up to £1 billion over a decade, prioritising research, design, compound semiconductors and industrial capabilities rather than attempting to reproduce every manufacturing stage domestically.

India is pursuing broader ecosystem development. Its Semicon 2.0 programme, approved on 15 July 2026, carries an outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. By October 2026, five of twelve approved semiconductor projects had commenced commercial production, according to the Indian government’s November disclosure.

These figures cannot be ranked as though they represented comparable completed investments. Public subsidies, programme outlays, mobilised private capital and commercial production are different economic categories.

The underlying choice is whether public expenditure creates capabilities that domestic industries can use competitively, or merely increases manufacturing capacity whose future commercial demand remains uncertain.

The Financial System Is Becoming Exposed to the Same AI Revenue Assumptions
Industrial concentration is accompanied by a less visible financial concentration.

In its October 2026 Global Financial Stability Report, the International Monetary Fund examined 14 publicly disclosed circular AI financing transactions since 2023. It identified approximately US$300 billion in equity investments, US$650 billion in debt and US$1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments. About US$320 billion of the debt was attributed to investees within those arrangements.

These amounts cannot be added into a single investment total. They describe different financial instruments and contractual obligations. Their significance lies instead in the relationships connecting investors, infrastructure suppliers, customers and creditors.

A technology company may finance an AI developer that purchases computing services from the same commercial ecosystem. During expansion, rising expected revenues support valuations, financing and additional infrastructure orders. During a correction, the same relationships can transmit weaker demand, falling asset values and tighter credit conditions simultaneously.

The IMF identifies this interaction as a source of wrong-way risk: exposures that deteriorate together when the underlying commercial assumptions fail.

The consequences extend into international trade. Reduced infrastructure spending can weaken demand for advanced processors, memory, servers and electrical equipment. Manufacturers may then revise their investment programmes, while financing constraints affect companies further upstream.

This is why the financial sustainability of AI investment cannot be assessed through revenue growth alone. Utilisation, operating margins, depreciation, electricity costs, financing obligations and future equipment replacement determine whether infrastructure generates sufficient economic returns.

An AI investment correction would not have to originate in trade policy to produce an international trade shock.

The Next 24 Months Will Determine Who Absorbs the Adjustment
Between November 2026 and November 2028, the decisive issue will be whether the present expansion converts capital expenditure into sustainable commercial returns before financing conditions, infrastructure bottlenecks or technology restrictions force an adjustment.

Three developments will be particularly consequential: the relationship between AI infrastructure spending and realised profitability; the ability of semiconductor and electricity suppliers to deliver operational capacity; and the direction of export-control and digital-trade policy.

The WTO’s 2027 merchandise trade growth forecast of 4.1% remains conditional on the continuation of supportive investment and broader economic conditions. It is not a guarantee of a technology-led expansion through 2031.

For the United States, the cost of miscalculation would fall on technology investors, infrastructure borrowers and companies whose investment programmes depend on sustained computing demand. For China, it would affect the returns on semiconductor industrial financing and the competitiveness of domestic technological substitutes. In Europe, poorly targeted subsidies could impose fiscal costs while leaving critical upstream dependencies unresolved. Italy’s Catania programme, France’s Crolles investment and Germany’s Dresden project will ultimately be judged by qualified production, customer demand and commercially sustainable output—not approved funding alone.

The cost of inaction would be distributed differently. Manufacturers lacking affordable access to advanced inputs would face higher production costs or delayed modernisation. Electricity users could confront infrastructure constraints and associated financing burdens. Lenders and institutional investors would remain exposed to concentrated commercial assumptions, while governments could face pressure to support projects whose expected returns have weakened.

Artificial intelligence is not converting protectionist governments into free traders. It is forcing them to confront the economic price of protection.

The distinction that will matter over the next 12–24 months is whether governments protect genuinely critical industrial capabilities or subsidise expensive substitutes for international production networks that remain indispensable. The first can improve resilience. The second can transfer technological risk onto taxpayers, industrial customers and the financial system without eliminating the underlying dependence.

text:
Engineering Wednesday: 

What The Sopranos Can Teach Us About Who Controls American Technology

Ever watch The Sopranos? There's something about Tony Soprano's approach to running a business that makes for an interesting thought experiment about what has happened inside parts of the American technology industry.

Imagine Tony and his associates gain control of a successful technology company. They need software engineers, network architects, cybersecurity specialists, database administrators, and people who understand the systems keeping the business operational.

But Tony has another requirement that might matter more to him than technical qualifications: he wants people he can trust to protect the organization and avoid questioning how decisions are made.

Would Tony advertise every position widely and hire the strongest independent candidate? Or would he prefer people recruited through established relationships, people whose careers and livelihoods depend on staying in his good graces?

Suppose the law requires him to advertise certain openings. He could comply with the formal requirements while making the recruitment process difficult for outsiders to discover or navigate. The paperwork might suggest an open competition even when management has already identified its preferred candidate.

Now imagine that the company operates in an industry where access to skilled labor, immigration policy, government contracts, and regulatory decisions can influence profitability. Tony would have another incentive: cultivate relationships with the people who write and enforce the rules. Through groups like ITServe Alliance and the Chamber of Commerce.

Political contributions, lobbying, and personal access could become tools for protecting the organization's interests.

This is a fictional illustration, not evidence that American technology companies operate like organized crime. However, it would explain so much.

It raises an important question about real institutions:

What happens when the people controlling employment opportunities also influence the rules governing recruitment, immigration sponsorship, and access to technical careers?

The Value of a Dependent Workforce

American technology companies employ engineers and technical professionals from around the world. Many are exceptionally capable, contribute to important innovations, and help American businesses compete internationally.

That isn't in dispute.

But employer-sponsored immigration introduces a relationship that deserves closer examination.

A worker whose legal status depends on employment may face consequences beyond losing a paycheck when that employment ends. H-1B workers have portability protections and certain grace periods, but changing employers can still involve legal expenses, uncertainty, and significant personal disruption.

That dependence can alter the balance of power between an employer and an employee.

An American software engineer who disagrees with management may resign and seek another position without jeopardizing immigration status. A foreign engineer working under an employer-dependent arrangement may have additional considerations before making the same decision.

That doesn't mean the foreign engineer is less competent, less ethical, or less willing to challenge questionable practices. It means the employment structure can impose different costs on exercising professional independence.

And in engineering, professional independence matters.

An engineer must be able to question unsafe designs, challenge unrealistic project schedules, identify security vulnerabilities, and report problems that management would rather not discuss.

Anyone who has spent much time in product development knows how uncomfortable those conversations can become when a launch date, contract milestone, or executive commitment is already on the calendar.

Now imagine having to weigh those professional responsibilities against the possibility of losing not only your job but also your ability to remain in the country.

That's a management incentive worth examining, regardless of whether employers deliberately exploit it.

When Recruiting Becomes a Closed Network

The next question concerns access to employment.

Anyone who has spent time applying for senior engineering or technology positions has probably encountered a job posting that seemed unusually specific.

Sometimes there's a perfectly legitimate explanation. The employer needs specialized experience, a particular certification, or familiarity with an existing system.

Other times, the requirements appear so narrowly written that you wonder whether the company already knows whom it intends to hire.

That distinction matters when immigration sponsorship is involved.

Some employment-based immigration programs require employers to meet wage, recruitment, or labor-certification requirements. The details differ substantially between H-1B sponsorship and permanent labor certification.

For certain permanent labor-certification applications, employers must conduct recruitment and demonstrate that qualified, available U.S. workers were not improperly excluded.

Those requirements exist to protect the domestic labor market.

But completing the paperwork isn't necessarily proof that recruitment was genuinely competitive.

The Department of Justice and Department of Labor have pursued cases involving discriminatory recruitment, improper hiring preferences, and violations of employment-related immigration requirements.

That establishes that abuses can occur. It does not establish that they are widespread throughout the technology industry.

Still, it raises questions worth investigating.

Are technical positions genuinely accessible to qualified American applicants? Are hiring managers using objective selection criteria? Are recruitment requirements being followed? Are qualified candidates being rejected because of their citizenship or immigration status when the law prohibits that distinction?

And perhaps most importantly, who controls the hiring process once a particular management group becomes established?

How Control Can Become Self-Reinforcing

Here's where the Sopranos analogy becomes particularly interesting.

Tony wouldn't necessarily need to own every business in New Jersey to exercise influence over them. He would need trusted people occupying positions where they could make important decisions.

The same general principle applies to organizational control, without implying that the people involved are engaged in criminal conduct.

A senior technology executive influences hiring decisions. Those hires eventually become managers. Managers influence promotions, contractor selection, technical assignments, and future recruitment.

Over time, an organization can develop a network of professional relationships that strongly influences who gets opportunities.

There's nothing inherently improper about hiring people you know and trust. Referrals are common throughout engineering, and experienced teams often recruit former colleagues because they understand their capabilities.

The concern arises when those relationships begin replacing genuine competition, objective qualifications, and transparent advancement.

An organization can become difficult for outsiders to enter even without anyone explicitly deciding to exclude them.

Now add employer-sponsored immigration, where some employees may have additional reasons to avoid challenging management, and the potential imbalance becomes more complicated.

This is one possible mechanism through which control can become concentrated. It is not proof that a coordinated takeover of American IT companies has occurred.

Establishing that would require evidence about hiring patterns, management appointments, recruitment decisions, and the treatment of qualified applicants.

The Caste Question 

Let's be blunt here... and watch the replies for the Izzat that follows.

There's another dimension that deserves examination, particularly in an industry with substantial international recruitment.

In Tony's fictional organization, a trusted associate might eventually become a made man, gaining status and authority through loyalty and relationships.

In a rigid caste hierarchy, social position can be inherited rather than earned. Education, technical accomplishment, and professional experience do not necessarily eliminate discrimination.

Caste discrimination has been documented as a concern in some South Asian diaspora workplaces, including allegations involving American technology companies. In fact, in the early 1900's it was pointed out by the colonizers as a serious issue where they were exporting labor to East Africa and the Carribean.

Recently and Domestically- The California Civil Rights Department brought a prominent case involving allegations of caste discrimination at Cisco Systems.

Where caste-based discrimination occurs, it creates another barrier to fair competition.

Who receives mentoring? Who gets promoted? Who is selected for management? Can an employee challenge discriminatory treatment without risking professional retaliation?

These are legitimate questions for any workplace where inherited social hierarchies may influence employment decisions.

And when discriminatory relationships overlap with immigration dependence, employees may face additional difficulties challenging the people controlling their careers.

Back to the Sopranos reference is Tony backfilling his open roles to anyone but his connected Italian relatives that have his back and are grateful for the job? We all know once they are in the family they cannot leave.

The appropriate response is to examine conduct and evidence, not assume that someone's nationality or ancestry determines how they behave.

Why American Technology Deserves Particular Attention

Technology companies are not ordinary businesses.

Their systems increasingly support banking, healthcare, communications, manufacturing, transportation, national defense, and critical infrastructure.

The people managing those systems make decisions with consequences extending far beyond their employers.

Consider cybersecurity.

A security engineer who identifies a serious vulnerability must be able to report it, even when doing so delays a product release or embarrasses management.

Consider software quality.

An engineer responsible for a critical application must be able to challenge inadequate testing, unrealistic schedules, or technical decisions that introduce unnecessary risks.

And consider artificial intelligence.

Companies are increasingly integrating AI into systems that influence employment, financial decisions, healthcare, and access to information.

We should want engineers working on those systems who can exercise independent professional judgment.

If employment arrangements make workers reluctant to question management, that creates a potential organizational risk regardless of where those workers were born.

If recruitment operates through closed networks, qualified applicants may lose opportunities.

If promotions depend more on personal relationships than technical competence, companies may overlook capable leaders.

None of these problems requires a conspiracy. Ordinary organizational incentives can produce undesirable outcomes when nobody is measuring or challenging them.

Follow the Political Money

There's another part of the story that deserves attention.

Major technology companies and industry organizations spend substantial resources lobbying Congress and federal agencies.

They advocate on immigration policy, workforce availability, government contracting, artificial intelligence, intellectual property, and regulation.

Lobbying isn't inherently corrupt. Businesses have legitimate reasons to explain their needs to lawmakers.

But the public has equally legitimate reasons to examine the relationship between corporate interests and the laws governing employment.

When an employer argues that America has a shortage of qualified technical workers, what evidence supports that claim?

Are the shortages concentrated in particular specialties, locations, or experience levels?

What wages are employers offering?

How many qualified domestic applicants are available?

And how do immigration programs affect wages, recruitment practices, and opportunities for American graduates and experienced professionals?

These questions deserve answers grounded in labor-market data rather than corporate press releases or political slogans.

The same scrutiny should apply to domestic staffing companies, offshore outsourcing arrangements, and foreign-worker recruitment.

The issue is whether employment practices reward technical competence and comply with the law.

Who Ultimately Controls American IT?

The Sopranos analogy is useful because it directs attention toward control rather than appearances.

An organization doesn't need to own every employee to exercise substantial influence over careers. It can control hiring, sponsorship, promotions, assignments, professional references, contractor relationships, and access to future opportunities.

Those mechanisms exist in legitimate businesses for legitimate reasons.

They can also be misused.

And if we're going to explain how management and employment opportunities have become concentrated within particular networks in some technology organizations, we need to examine the mechanisms rather than assume the answer.

That means looking at recruitment records, visa sponsorship practices, management appointments, compensation, promotion patterns, discrimination complaints, and documented enforcement actions.

It also means recognizing that a large foreign-born workforce is not, by itself, evidence of wrongdoing or a coordinated takeover.

American engineers deserve genuine access to positions for which they're qualified. Foreign engineers deserve protection against exploitation and discrimination. Employers deserve access to specialized talent when they comply with the law.

Those interests aren't mutually exclusive.

The question isn't whether internationally trained engineers belong in American technology. The question is whether the institutions controlling technical employment are structured to reward competence, protect independent judgment, and provide fair opportunities, or whether some recruitment and sponsorship arrangements give established management networks too much influence over who gets hired and who advances.

That's a question worth investigating.

And unlike Tony Soprano's fictional business arrangements, we have employment records, regulatory requirements, and federal enforcement agencies capable of helping establish the facts.

I'd rather see those records than another argument about whether American engineers are qualified to do the jobs they've been doing for decades.

Final thought... If Tony was caught would he start to comply or would he find a way to bribe, replace, or remove whoever was interfering with his business? 

Chief

References:

California Civil Rights Department. (2020). Department of Fair Employment and Housing files lawsuit against Cisco Systems, Inc. and two managers for discrimination, harassment, and retaliation.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. (2025). H-1B specialty occupations.

U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division. (n.d.). Protecting U.S. workers initiative.

U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration. (n.d.). Permanent labor certification (PERM).

U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division. (n.d.). H-1B program.

text:
NFL Week 9 Review ✍️

My thoughts on all the games (entering Monday) with statistical analysis, upgrades, and downgrades for each team. Thank you for reading.

Jaguars 33, Ravens 10 (TNF)
Jacksonville dominated the box score (+1.6 net YPP, +14% net SR) and won turnovers (3-1). The game was played in a monsoon which did not help the Ravens limited offense. Joe Fagnano had one of the worst quarterback performances I’ve ever seen in the NFL. He made Nathan Peterman look like Joe Montana. The Jags continue to look like a balanced unit on both ends. Liam Coen has had an incredible impact on Trevor Lawrence and he has a complete grasp of the offense in year two of the system. On Monday the Jaguars went all in, trading for DT Jordan Davis, S Jessie Bates, and another depth DT Davon Godchaux. The Davis deal was a blockbuster with Jacksonville sending their 2027 1st round pick and a 2nd round pick in 2029. They also sent their 2nd round pick in 2027 to Atlanta for Bates. Just a complete shove from GM James Gladstone who obviously feels like he has the right pieces in place to win the Super Bowl this season. Hard to argue with him. Jacksonville also has one of the easiest remaining schedules in the AFC and is in contention for the No. 1 seed. Massive upgrade not only for this win but also for the moves they made on Monday. I’m going to give the Ravens a 6-point boost with Jacoby Brissett taking over as starting quarterback. He is that much better than Fagnano, who is truly awful.

Bengals 34, Falcons 17 (Madrid)
Cincinnati won the box score (+1.4 net YPP, +6.4% net SR) and won turnovers (1-0). Joe Burrow continues to look like the MVP of the league. He leads the NFL in EPA and TDs. They continued to lean into their passing game with a 12% PROE (pass rate over expected). Burrow was pressured on nearly 40% of dropbacks but had nearly a 60% success rate when pressured. Since Week 3, the Bengals rank 1st in EPA/dropback. Over the last three games, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have combined for 47 catches, 693 yards, and 8 touchdowns. The Falcons look like a total lemon despite having a decent day on the ground. Michael Penix struggled especially on early downs. They committed too many penalties and the defense could not get off the field on 3rd downs. Then on Monday they traded away their best safety for draft capital. It feels like full sell mode for Atlanta despite only being a half-game out of first place in the horrific NFC South. Upgrade Cincinnati. Bigger downgrade Atlanta.

Saints 23, Browns 22 (OT)
New Orleans won the box score (+0.4 net YPP, +10.4% net SR) and turnovers were even (1-1). Jordyn Tyson (4 receptions, 30 yards) made his NFL debut and was on a snap count but had a key fumble near the goal line which took points off the board. New Orleans only went 2-for-5 scoring TDs in the RZ. I expect to see more of Tyson going forward and he adds another explosive element next to Chris Olave. Shedeur Sanders had his moments in his first start of the season for Deshaun Watson (concussion) but he looked rattled under pressure and took five sacks. To be fair, both of his touchdown passes also came when facing pressure but I would argue those were also incredible individual efforts by KC Concepion, who scored his first career TD, and Harold Fanin Jr. who made one of the most incredible plays you will see to almost tie the game in OT. I liked the decision by Todd Monken to go for the win after Fanin scored, but the play call was bad and even if they converted there was a holding penalty against Cleveland. I think Watson is still a better option at QB than Sanders. The ceiling and floor are both higher. Sanders still looks like a rookie. Tyler Shough also looked shaky at times in the pocket and his broken non-throwing hand is an issue with exchanges. If he stays healthy the upside is certainly there with this offense especially with Tyson and LT Kelvin Banks Jr. back in the mix. But New Orleans also is giving up too much pressure and Shough took 5 sacks in this game. No upgrade or downgrade for either team. I will upgrade Cleveland slightly if Watson returns to the lineup next week.

Cowboys 27 Colts 23
Dallas won the box score (+2.7 net YPP, +1.6% net SR) but turnovers were even (2-2). The Cowboys were highly explosive with Dak Prescott (335 yards, 2 TDs) and CeeDee Lamb (10 catches, 195 yards) doing their thing. However Lamb committed a bad TO in the RZ which made this game feel a lot closer than it actually was. The Cowboys defense was still pretty leaky and allowed a 55-yard explosive to Ashton Dulin on a missed tackle. Tyler Warren (4 catches, 44 yards) was also consistent and the run game produced enough to keep the Cowboys honest. Daniel Jones predictably threw a late INT to seal the game. The Colts announced that he won’t be traded despite some inquiries. The Cowboys receiver situation continues to be something to monitor with George Pickens (hamstring) sitting and KaVonte Turpin (ribs) missing his third straight game. Jake Ferguson also left the game with a knee injury. Jerry Jones said the team won’t be making any major trades but I trust Jerry as far as I can throw him. Dallas needs to clean up the penalties (14-153) if they want to be taken seriously in a winnable NFC East. They also have to play better on defense (30th in EPA per play allowed) but that is probably a more difficult task than making fewer unforced errors. I continue to feel like I have a pretty good read on this Cowboys team. Fade them against the teams that can move the ball and never lay more than a FG with them as a favorite. They pushed most numbers in this game as a 4-point favorite but there were some 4.5’s out there so some of you might have covered with Indy. Teasing the Colts through 10 was a very strong play and you were never outside of the number. No upgrade or downgrade for either team. I have the Cowboys essentially rated as an average team at the moment, and I feel comfortable with that rating. I have the Colts as one of the worst teams in the NFL, slightly ahead of the Browns. Even if they trade Jonathan Taylor this week I won’t downgrade them much if at all. He only got 13 carries in this game and it’s clear he isn’t a big part of the plan anymore.

Broncos 26, Panthers 21
Denver’s luck train continues. Carolina won the box score (+0.9 net YPP, +3.6% net SR) but lost turnovers (1-2). I still don’t understand how they overturned the RZ INT that clearly was trapped against the ground. The correct call should have been stands. If it was called an INT on the field I would have understood why they would have stayed with the call. But overturning that is pure madness. It was also clearly DPI that they ref missed. Carolina got screwed on that play. Bo Nix continues to pull games out of his ass for no apparent reasons. The Broncos have won 17 straight one score games and have covered in 7 straight one score games. The Panthers continued to beat themselves and lost 30.36 combined EPA to turnovers, sacks, and penalties. Bryce Young got stripped with Carolina driving late for the game-winning score. He continues to play small in the pocket in front of a bad offensive line. There are some injuries starting to pile up for Denver with WR Jaylen Waddle (concussion) and Riley Moss (concussion) both getting knocked out of the game. Denver is already dealing with injuries in the secondary with both starting safeties (Talanoa Hufanga, Brnadon Jones) missing this game. That is something to watch going forward. TE Darren Waller (8 catches, 10 targets, 90 yards, TD) has been a bright spot for Carolina. As long as he stays healthy I expect him to keep making plays especially in the RZ. Tet McMillan has been held in check with 56 yards or fewer in the last three games. No upgrade or downgrade for either team. This was a fugazi win for the Broncos, their second one in the last three weeks (Seahawks).

Lions 19, Dolphins 9
Detroit won the box score (+0.2 net YPP, +15% net SR) and turnovers were even. I was impressed with the Dolphins defense generating their highest pressure rate of the season (26.7%) moving Jared Goff off his spot and forcing some bad throws, one led to an INT. The Miami offense is trending in the wrong direction likely because of an obvious injury to Malik Willis who only had 2 runs for 7 yards. If his mobility continues to be limited this offense has a major ceiling as they are horrible in the passing game. Not only is Willis inaccurate as a passer but their receivers are inexperienced and had a ton of drops, including a bad one on 4th down by Caleb Douglas which would have kept the drive alive in the final minutes. The Lions looked a step slow on offense and gained a season low 272 yards. This makes sense considering they are coming off a physical game against a division rival with an incredible aggressive defense. I think they will be fine and I’m not going to overreact to one bad performance. They also head to Germany next week for a game against the Patriots. So they might have been looking ahead to the trip. Slight downgrade Miami. I’m already low on them but if Willis is hurt this offense will go in the tank. No upgrade for Detroit.

Rams 20, Commanders 13
The Commanders won YPP (5.5 to 4.8) but lost SR (38.6% to 43.1%) and turnovers were even (2-2). Matthew Stafford continued to show his age. He completed just 5-of-11 passes for 37 yards with a -11.1% CPOE (completion rate over expected) when facing pressure. He also will be without WR Puka Nacua for at least the next 4 weeks after he was placed on IR Monday with an MCL and PCL injury. The Rams are already without DaVante Adams. Their defense looked electric with Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald seeing the field together for the first time. They will have to rely on their run game and defense to get them through this difficult time without Adams and Nacua in the lineup. I would expect them to be active in trying to acquire a WR before the trade deadline this week. The Commanders continue to beat themselves in key moments. They have no semblance of a run game to help out Jayden Daniels. They had multiple opportunities to win and cover this game but could do neither. You can’t trust them against real teams. Slight downgrade for the Rams who will be significantly limited on offense until they get healthy at WR. Also a slight downgrade for the Commanders.

Giants 19, Eagles 11
New York won an ugly box score (+0.5 net YPP, +6% net SR) and won turnovers (2-0). Joe Mitlon was awful for Philly. He had a worse EPA number than Joe Fagnano. Both teams struggled to move the ball especially on early downs. The JJ McCarthy hip injury looked painful, Jameis Winston came in and threw a TD pass and McCarthy came back later in the game but neither QB was able to do much. There were 13 combined sacks in this game and it was a brutal watch on both ends. The Giants managed to cover as a road favorite and it stayed way under. I still think McCarthy is the best option for the Giants at QB right now but I’m not sure if he’s fully healthy. Winston is incredibly volatile and is a great fade especially after a good performance. The Giants should get back RB Cam Skattebo next week which will give them some stability in the run game. On Monday the Eagles traded away the anchor of their defense DT Jordan Davis to Jacksonville in exchange for a 2027 first round pick. I think this is a major red flag for Vic Fangio, who will likely be fired at the end of the season or possibly sooner. I think Nick Sirianni will survive this season and be back in 2027. Just a hunch. No upgrade for the Giants as I need more info about their QB situation. Big downgrade for the Eagles who are clearly punting on the rest of the season.

Chiefs 35, Jets 12
Belt to ass. Kansas City won the box score (+2.4 net YPP, +17.6% net SR) but lost TOs (1-2). The biggest story in this game was the Patrick Mahomes elbow injury, which looked serious, but he didn’t miss any snaps. WR Xavier Worthy (left hamstring) also got hurt in the 4th quarter on a non-contact injury and starting RT Jaylon Moore (right ankle) also left the game. I think the Chiefs will be active in the trade markets this week looking for depth on offense, especially at WR. Breece Hall (15 carries, 61 yards, 3 catches, 26 yards) returned from injury but didn’t create much of a spark. Braelon Allen (8 carries, 33 yards) was also held in check. The Jets offense really missed WR Garrett Wilson (concussion) and Geno Smith (156 yards, 5.2 YPA) had his worst game since the loss in Chicago. Omar Cooper also reinjured his ankle and is probably out next week which makes their receiver group even more limited. The good news for the Jets is the Colts keep losing and they now have two of the top six picks in the 2027 draft. Keeping the young players healthy and getting them experience while continuing to lose games and improve the team’s draft stock should be the Jets main focus in the second half of the regular season. No upgrade for Kansas City because this was a cakewalk game and the Mahomes injury along with their other offensive injuries are a concern. Slight downgrade for the Jets. Even bigger downgrade if Wilson doesn’t return next week.

Texans 44, Chargers 22
Another belt to ass special. Houston won the box score (+3.0 net YPP, +9.1% net SR) and won turnovers (2-1). CJ Stroud showed the ceiling (384 yards, 5 TDs) and Tank Dell scored his first TD since December 2024. The bad vibes started early for the Chargers when Ladd McConkey had pregame back spasms and didn’t play. Justin Herbert continued to sink further. Considering the expectations entering the year it’s fair to call him the worst player in the NFL this season. This was one of my easiest wins in the Circa contest last week. I don’t understand how anyone can back this Chargers team right now, especially getting less than a TD. I made that mistake last week against the Rams and I swore to myself I wouldn’t do it again for the rest of the year, especially if Herbert continues to be the starting QB. I’m still a believer in this Houston team and they have one of the easiest remaining schedules in the league. Over 9.5 wins is still a possibility especially if they can beat the Browns, Colts, and Ravens the next 3 weeks and get back to 6-5. I don’t think they can catch the Jags in the division but they have an outside shot of being a wild card team in the AFC. The biggest concern is the secondary with Reed Blankenship out but the front seven is elite and they have two stud pass rushers in Wil Anderson and Danielle Hunter. I trust DeMeco Ryans as a defensive playcaller and I think they have way more talent than https://t.co/hp2UjHKoAR current 22nd EPA per play allowed ranking indicates. Slight upgrade Houston. Slightly bigger downgrade Chargers. I’ve now dropped them over 8 points since Week 1 (+2.6 to -5.9).

49ers 38, Raiders 17
San Francisco won the box score (+1.2 net YPP, +9.6% net SR) and won turnovers (5-1). This was the worst Kirk Cousins performance of the season. The Raiders were held to their lowest EPA per play and early downs EPA number of the season. If you want to credit the Niners defense for that I won’t argue with you, but I also think Cousins has a very limited ceiling and the mystery of this Klint Kubiak offense is now gone with teams having nine weeks of tape on him. It doesn’t look like they will turn to Fernando Mendoza anytime soon, but I would expect that move to happen at some point, likely after the Week 13 bye. Vegas plays the Chargers, Titans and Cardinals along with the Broncos and Chiefs in their final five games. That’s a good tuneup for the No.1 overall pick with a couple of tough divisional opponents sandwiched around some cupcakes. The Niners offense continues to hum along despite being without Mike Evans, which I thought was going to be a big loss for them. They leaned on the run game in this one with CMC (18 carries, 68 yards, TD), Kaelon Black (11 carries, 70 yards) and even Brock Purdy (7 carries, 40 yards, TD) contributing. Second year WR Jordan Watkins (4 receptions, 86 yards, TD) looked explosive as did George Kittle (4 catches, 58 yards) and CMC also chipped in with a receiving TD. The biggest difference for the Niners this year is defense. They rank 12th in EPA per play after finishing 25th in that category last season. Obviously DC Raheem Morris has had a huge impact. Slight upgrade Niners. Hopefully they get Evans back soon but clearly they are fine without him. I have the Niners as my top rated team in the NFC. Slightly bigger downgrade Vegas.

Seahawks 17, Cardinals 3
Seattle won the box score (+1.2 net YPP, +1.8% net SR) and neither team committed a turnover although it sure looked like Trey McBride fumbled but the refs blew the play dead for forward progress and didn’t review it, which is dumb. I don’t understand why replay exists if we can’t fix obvious errors like that. Arizona kicked a FG on their opening drive and then got shutout for the rest of the game. Credit the Seattle defense for playing well on a short week off a loss. Drew Lock didn’t look great, he was clearly hampered with an oblique injury. He said he will play next week. If he doesn’t then it’ll be a pretty big downgrade to Jalen Milroe who would be making his first NFL start. I don’t know when Sam Darnold will return from his quad injury. Newly acquired LG Quenton Nelson also had knee surgery this week and is probably out at least a couple more weeks. Starting LT Charles Cross is also still sidelined. The entire left side of the Seahawks offensive line is a mess right now. In fact their entire offensive is basically JSN and a bunch of traffic cones. I don’t know what the answer is for them right now unless they can magically get the run game going with Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price. The good news is they get another cakewalk this week against the Raiders before their bye. Hopefully they get healthy before they return for a huge game at the Niners in Week 11. Arizona is a full sell right now. They will likely be without QB Gardner Minshew for the rest of the season after he injured his UCL in this game but played through it in the second half. That means Carson Beck will make his first career start next week against the Rams before a trip to Arrowhead the following week. Yikes. I thought Beck looked good in preseason but this is obviously a completely different animal. Arizona is also depleted at WR with Michael Wilson injuring his neck in this game and will be out for the season. Jeremiyah Love is also still banged up. What a disaster for Mike LaFleur who has done a lot with a little his first season in the desert. No upgrade for Seattle as we await word on their QB situation. Big downgrade Arizona going from Minshew to Beck. At least 3 points, probably more.

Packers 45, Patriots 27
Green Bay won the box score (+1.2 net YPP, +2.7% net SR) and dominated turnovers (4-0). Drake Maye had his head up his ass most of the game. The first pick he threw was one of the worst throws I’ve ever seen him make, which is saying something. I’m convinced they could have brought Tom Brady down from the booth and he would have played better than Maye did in this game. Jordan Love was in his bag and showed no fear targeting Pats top CB Christian Gonzalez (9 catches for 177 yards, TD) who got torched in this game. Love his a legit MVP candidate. He was 10/10 for 146 yards and a TD against the blitz as the Packers scored 45 points despite not running it that well. Speaking of the run game, Josh Jacobs fractured his finger. I’m not sure if he’ll play through it or not but he wasn’t that effective this season even with all 10 healthy digits. At some point Green Bay will need to play with balance as teams will take away the deep ball but that clearly hasn’t happened yet. The Packers defense is also 7th in EPA per play allowed and should get Micah Parsons back soon. Scary. The NFC North is so good this season but you have to consider the ceiling for Green Bay just as high as any of the other teams because of Love’s ability to push the ball downfield. I still think the Bears roster is better now that they have Jeffrey Simmons up front, but the Pack are right there. Big upgrade Green Bay. Big downgrade New England. I can’t take this team seriously without their main weapons on the outside and Maye not taking care of the ball.

Bears 27, Bucs 24
Chicago won the box score (+0.7 net YPP, +3.1% net SR) but lost turnovers (2-5). Chicago really struggled on offense in the second half failing to score a point. Their only points were a pick six and the GW FG. Credit the Bucs defense which is a top tier unit. After getting punked in the first quarter they settled down and created a ton of havoc plays especially in the second half. They dominated the Chicago run game and forced Caleb Williams into some poor decisions under pressure. Chicago’s defense also did their job with 10 pressures on 27 four-man rushes. The biggest issue I had in this game was Tampa’s conservative game plan. They had more than twice as many runs as throws on first down and failed to capitalize on the turnover margin. Here is how they fared after Williams four INTs: turnover on downs, punt, field goal, pick six. Similar to basketball, scoring points off turnovers is almost as vital as creating the turnovers themselves. The Bucs clearly do not trust their outside WRs or they rely too heavily on Bucky Irving, maybe a mix of both. It’s not like Baker Mayfield is a rookie. I don’t understand the plan OC Zac Robinson is trying to accomplish. The Bears winning despite being a minus-3 in turnovers is the worst TO margin in a Bears win since the Dennis Green rant game in 2006. If you want to crown their ass then crown em! I’m not ready to crown this Chicago team just yet unless Caleb Williams can find more consistency with his game, especially in the second half and when things aren’t going his way. But the talent is certainly there and the defense is a top 10 unit, maybe top 5, with Simmons in the middle. No upgrade or downgrade for either team after this weird game. I already upgraded Chicago significantly last week and I think the Bucs defense will keep them in a lot of games down the stretch despite their conservative plan on offense.

CINTAS $CTAS IS NEAR A HIGH WITH THE FTC CIRCLING:

The Quality-Value Len5 is watching Cintas (CTAS) at $222.36, -$4.05 / -1.79% on Friday.

Cintas holds the #10 seat on the Quality-Value Len5 for its business, and at about 40 times this year's forecast profit the price offers no discount. The Cincinnati company rents and cleans work uniforms and runs first-aid and fire-safety programs, and its latest quarter carried a record 51.5% gross margin. On October 27 Semafor reported that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) means to sue to block Cintas's purchase of a smaller rival, UniFirst (UNF) at $235.40, -$7.80 / -3.21% on Friday. Cintas has lost 1.6% since then. UniFirst has lost 15.8%, and its holders have far more riding on the deal. The deal cannot close before December 11 unless the FTC ends its review sooner.

- Quality-Value Len5: #10, partial. It wants a durable business at a discount, and Cintas has the durable half: 8.9% organic growth in the quarter to August 31, with acquisitions and currency stripped out, and an operating margin, what it keeps from each sales dollar after running the business, of 23.6%, from 22.7%. At about 40 times the $5.45 to $5.54 a share it forecasts for the year to May 2027, the discount half is missing. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: that margin falling back under 22.7%.
- Momentum Len5: partial, not a pick. It wants a stock near its high with gains agreeing over one, three and six months; Cintas closed 4.8% under the $233.46 it touched on Thursday, its highest price in a year, and up 13.5%, 10.0% and 31.3%. A close above $233.46 on its own news would bring it into view for the Momentum Len5.
- Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: not a fit. It wants a price well under a cautious value of what the business earns, and Cintas costs about 44 times the past year's profit. A far lower price with profit intact would bring it into view for the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5.
- Hypergrowth Len5: not a fit. It wants sales multiplying; Cintas's revenue rose 10.9%. Growth several times that pace would put it on the Hypergrowth Len5.
- Income Len5: not a fit. It wants cash paid to owners that matters against the price, and the $0.52 quarterly dividend is 0.9% of Friday's close. A payout several times larger against the price would put it on the Income Len5.
- Quality Len5: passes. It wants a profit with debt under the owners' stake: $551.7M of quarterly profit, and $2.43B of debt against $5.20B of equity on August 31. Borrowing for the deal's roughly $2.8B cash half that pushed debt past that equity would knock it off the Quality Len5.

Each UniFirst share gets $155 in cash plus 0.7720 Cintas shares, worth $326.66 at Friday's close. The FTC said in a statement that it has not voted.
- UniFirst at Friday's close: $91.26 under the deal's value.
- October 27: Cintas -4.9%; UniFirst -10.5%.
If antitrust review ends the deal, Cintas owes UniFirst $350M, nearly two-thirds of a quarter's profit, and the merger agreement commits both companies to fight a challenge in court. UniFirst is on none of the Len5es we weigh; at 39 times the past year's profit, its price carries no discount.

Cintas keeps its Quality-Value seat on a record margin, and at 40 times profit, buyers already pay for that margin. The December 17 report, tentative, is the first since the Semafor story, and organic growth well under 8.9% would cost Cintas more than any ruling on UniFirst.

Not investment advice.

🚨🍎 Breaking: Mets Schedule In-Person Meeting With Tarik Skubal Next Week! Steve Cohen Is Getting Serious! 🔥⚾

Mets fans, this is the news we've been waiting for!

According to MLB insider Jon Heyman of the New York Post, the New York Mets have scheduled an in-person meeting with superstar left-hander Tarik Skubal next week in #California!

And while an actual contract agreement is still a long way from being guaranteed, this is certainly an encouraging development for a franchise desperately searching for a legitimate ace to lead its pitching staff.

🔥 Even Better? Heyman Believes the Mets Are the Favorites!

During an appearance on MLB Network on Monday, Heyman indicated that he currently favors the Mets in the Skubal sweepstakes.

That's a pretty significant statement, considering the competition #NewYork could face.

Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, are expected to meet with multiple interested organizations in #California, with the San Diego Padres among the teams showing interest.

The Los Angeles Dodgers, who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers at the 2026 trade deadline, are also expected to be involved.

And let's not forget potential interest from the #Giants, #Phillies, and #BlueJays.

But here's the difference: Steve Cohen has the financial firepower to separate the #Mets from everyone else! 💰

⚾ Skubal Is Exactly What This Rotation Needs!

We've been discussing Skubal here at Mets Junkies for quite some time, and my position hasn't changed one bit.

Tarik Skubal needs to be the Mets' No. 1 offseason priority!

Just look at what he brings to the table:

🏆 American League Cy Young Award winner in 2024 and 2025

🔥 2026 MLB Statistics:

12–7 record

2.72 ERA

0.96 WHIP

158⅔ innings pitched

26 starts

Approximately 10.6 strikeouts per nine innings

And here's what's especially exciting.

Imagine going into 2027 with Tarik Skubal and Nolan McLean leading the Mets rotation!

You're talking about an established, dominant left-handed ace paired with one of the most exciting young pitchers in baseball.

Add Christian Scott and some of the organization's other promising young arms, and suddenly the outlook for this rotation changes dramatically.

💰 Steve Cohen Needs to Make Skubal an Offer He Can't Refuse!

There's no getting around the fact that Skubal is going to be extremely expensive.

He's expected to challenge the existing records for both total guaranteed money and average annual salary for a starting pitcher.

But if there's one owner in baseball capable of making that kind of financial commitment, it's Steve Cohen.

And after watching the Mets miss the postseason for the second consecutive year, I believe Cohen needs to make a statement.

This is not the offseason to get outbid for the pitcher you've identified as your top target!

We've previously discussed the possibility of going as high as $60 million annually for Skubal, and I still believe the Mets should seriously consider that type of aggressive offer if that's what it takes to land him.

Skubal turns 30 on November 20, meaning a substantial contract would cover several of what should be his prime remaining seasons.

⏳ Could a Deal Happen Before December?

Here's another interesting wrinkle.

With Major League Baseball facing a potential lockout when the current collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, there's speculation that Skubal could look to finalize his next contract before that deadline.

That could accelerate negotiations considerably.

And with the Mets scheduled to sit down with Skubal next week, they have an opportunity to make their pitch before the offseason potentially comes to a standstill.

Of course, this meeting doesn't mean Skubal is signing with the Mets.

But it's a meaningful step in the process, and it's encouraging to see the organization pursuing the biggest name on the free-agent market.

$AMPX Q3 2026 earnings: Amprius raises its sales plan, but cuts its profit target

Amprius is selling more drone batteries than ever in the United States, but rising development costs delayed its profit turnaround. The silicon-anode battery maker grew third-quarter revenue 83% from a year ago to $39.1 million as domestic sales more than doubled from last quarter. Chief executive Tom Stepien raised the full-year sales plan to $145 million and announced a $75 million U. S. defense contract to fund domestic production in 2028.

• Revenue: $𝟑𝟗.𝟏𝐌 (+83% from a year ago, +15% from Q2)
• U. S. revenue: $𝟏𝟐.𝟐𝐌 (2.3x last quarter (31% of sales))
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟓𝐌 (to $145M (+99% from 2025))
• Full-year Adjusted EBITDA outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 $𝟏.𝟓𝐌 (to at least $2.5M (from at least $4.0M))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because domestic defense wins strengthened the revenue case while an operating profit outlook cut confirmed our prior cost concerns. Higher research spending kept Adjusted EBITDA negative at -$1.0 million, forcing finance chief Ricardo C. Rodriguez to lower the full-year cash profit target. By our math, hitting the unchanged full-year gross margin and net loss goals still requires a jump to a 35% gross margin in the fourth quarter.

The question now is whether fourth-quarter gross margin can jump nearly eight percentage points to hit the untouched profit goals, or whether full-year net loss will miss too. Government grant credits and European pouch-cell orders could lift fourth-quarter margins, while lower-margin U. S. shipments and elevated research costs could hold them back. Fourth-quarter results and the quarterly filing's backlog and Ukraine disclosures will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐮𝐭
Amprius makes silicon-anode lithium-ion batteries that store up to twice the energy of standard graphite cells for drones and aircraft. To sell to the U. S. military, the battery maker must comply with the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a law restricting components from countries of concern.

U. S. revenue rose 2.3 times from last quarter to $12.2 million, reaching 31% of total sales by our math. The California group also won a $75 million U. S. Department of War contract, with $22.3 million already committed, "supporting the conversion of an existing battery production line with planned output of up to 12 million NDAA-compliant cells annually in 2028".

This award matters because U. S. defense rules require domestic or allied cell production by January 2028, and government money now pays for that capacity build. In addition, the $8.0 million of government grant income assumed in this year's outlook helps fund current domestic engineering work.

What to watch: December 2026 production startup on the expanded Fremont pilot line, funded by the Defense Innovation Unit. Starting on time will show that the team can install domestic electrode tools without delays before tackling the larger 2028 factory conversion.

🟢 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐒𝐢𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬
"Our third quarter results demonstrate the strength of our company’s technology leadership and our ability to convert growing customer demand into meaningful financial performance," chief executive Tom Stepien said. Quarterly sales reached $39.1 million, up 83% from a year ago and 15% from last quarter, prompting a third raise to the full-year revenue outlook.

Amprius launched SiCore 500, a second-generation silicon-anode battery cell that packs 500 watt-hours per kilogram and runs "on conventional lithium-ion manufacturing equipment". Previously, only its older SiMaxx cells reached that energy density, and they required custom tools at the Fremont pilot lab. The cell maker also expanded deliveries to German drone builder Quantum Systems and won orders for a solar stratospheric aircraft and a deep-sea defense vehicle.

Running a 500 watt-hour cell on standard machinery matters because outside contract factories can now mass-produce the highest-energy battery without custom equipment bottlenecks. What to watch: initial commercial shipments under the $100 million Stark Future electric-motorcycle contract in early 2027, which will test whether contract partners can deliver high-volume mobility orders alongside defense drones.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐑&𝐃 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐂𝐮𝐭
For three quarters, Amprius paired higher revenue targets with a steady full-year profit goal of at least $4.0 million in Adjusted EBITDA, which is operating cash profit before stock pay, depreciation, and one-time facility costs. This quarter, the battery maker cut that full-year target to at least $2.5 million while holding its full-year gross margin floor at 28%.

• Q3 Adjusted EBITDA: -$1.0 million, missing the +$3.4 million second-half quarterly pace implied by the old plan
• Research and development: $6.4 million, up 155% from a year ago and up 4.7 percentage points of revenue to 16.4%
• Selling, general, and administrative costs: $8.8 million, down 3.1 percentage points of revenue from a year ago to 22.6%
• Implied Q4 hurdles by our math: 34.8% gross margin, $5.6 million in Adjusted EBITDA, and $3.6 million in GAAP net profit

The cut matters because rising product development costs absorbed the gross profit gains from higher volume, leaving nine-month GAAP net loss at $13.6 million against a full-year loss cap of $10.0 million. Because gross margin dipped slightly from 27.3% in Q2 to 26.9% in Q3 as U. S. sales rose, reaching the full-year margin and net loss targets now requires a nearly eight-point margin jump in the final quarter.

What to watch: fourth-quarter gross margin and research spending in the full-year report. Anything below a 34.8% gross margin at the $43.3 million revenue implied by the outlook will cause the business to miss its 28% annual margin floor.

🔴🔴 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
"The third quarter once again proved the scalability of our fabless technology and process-owning strategy," finance chief Ricardo C. Rodriguez said, adding that the team meets demand "without the need for capital investment for manufacturing". Under this contract-manufacturing setup, partner factories build the cells while Amprius owns the silicon-anode process.

The cash flow statement cuts against that capital-light framing. By our math, capital spending on property and equipment jumped to $5.2 million in the third quarter, up from $1.8 million in Q2, bringing nine-month spending to $8.0 million against an annual cap of $10.0 million. At the same time, unpaid customer bills rose to $45.9 million — more than an entire quarter of sales — and inventory more than doubled since December to $15.9 million.

Together, inventory, prepaid items, and customer receivables consumed $13.0 million of free cash flow in the third quarter by our math, even though operating losses held steady. What to watch: fourth-quarter accounts receivable collections and capital spending, because another $13 million quarterly cash burn would push total cash below $50 million entering 2027.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing business and supply-chain risks could not be checked from the earnings release alone and await the quarterly filing or conference call.

• Ukraine revenue concentration: shipments to Ukraine-based customers made up 31% of Q2 sales; the quarterly filing's geographic note will show whether rapid U. S. growth reduced that exposure.
• Remaining performance obligations (backlog): sat at $36.5 million in June, covering just 1.1 times quarterly sales; the filing's contract footnote will show if multi-quarter order cover improved.
• NDAA component supplier contracts: Stepien pledged last quarter to sign all remaining compliant material suppliers by Q3; the conference call must confirm completion.
• China export controls and Berzelius reliance: Chinese battery export control suspensions expire in November 2026, and purchase volumes from related-party silicon supplier Berzelius remain undisclosed.
• Customer receivable concentration: two buyers accounted for 54% of unpaid bills in Q2; the filing's risk note will reveal whether the $45.9 million Q3 balance rests on the same pair.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔𝟏.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Cash reserves fell by $12.9 million during the third quarter and sit $30.1 million below year-end 2025. The nine-month decline includes a one-time $20.0 million payment in January to exit the Brighton, Colorado lease, partially offset by $25.5 million raised from warrant and stock option exercises.

𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝-𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟒𝟔.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The average share count rose 15.6% from a year ago and 2.0% from the second quarter. Warrant exercises brought in $14.2 million and employee stock options added $11.3 million across the first nine months, lifting common shares outstanding to 146.6 million at the end of September.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Combined current and long-term lease obligations rose slightly from $6.4 million in June but remain down 82% from $39.9 million at the end of 2025. Terminating the 15-year Colorado factory lease in January removed over $110 million in future commitments and left the balance sheet with zero debt.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏𝟒𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from At least $140.0 million
Raised. The full-year target moved up $5 million to $145 million, nearly doubling last year's sales. By our math, that leaves $43.3 million for Q4, up 11% from Q3 and 72% from a year ago. It is the third raise this year following increases of $5 million in May and $10 million in August.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝐀𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝟐𝟖%  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from At least 28%
Unchanged. Management kept the full-year gross margin floor at 28% after raising it from 25% last quarter. Because gross margin averaged 25.1% across the first nine months ($25.5 million on $101.7 million of sales), hitting 28% for the full year requires a 34.8% margin in Q4 by our math, nearly eight points above Q3.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: 𝐀𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭 $𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from At least $4.0 million
Cut. The battery maker lowered its full-year Adjusted EBITDA floor by $1.5 million (the reconciliation table prints a $2.7 million point estimate). With nine-month Adjusted EBITDA at -$3.1 million after Q3's -$1.0 million loss, reaching the $2.5 million floor requires $5.6 million in Q4 by our math, a 13% margin.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬: 𝐋𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 $𝟏𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
🠆 unchanged from Less than $10.0 million
Unchanged. The plan still caps the full-year GAAP net loss attributable to common stockholders at $10.0 million, including Q2's $1.9 million non-cash warrant charge. Because the nine-month loss has already reached $13.6 million, the outlook requires at least $3.6 million of positive GAAP net profit in Q4 by our math.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 $𝟎.𝟎𝟕  ⇄ reversing
🠅 raised from Under $0.08
Tightened by one cent. On the unchanged 143.4 million full-year weighted-average share count assumption, a $10.0 million net loss rounds to $0.07 per share. Nine-month loss per share already stands at $0.10, so meeting this cap depends on the same $3.6 million Q4 net profit swing.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞: 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 $𝟏𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from Under $10.0 million
Unchanged. Full-year property and equipment spending remains capped at $10.0 million. After spending $2.8 million in the first half and $5.2 million in Q3 by our math ($8.0 million across nine months), the cap leaves at most $2.0 million for Q4 as Fremont pilot-line installation wraps up.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭-𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐐𝟒 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩?
Nine-month gross margin is 25.1%, so the 28% full-year floor requires 34.8% in Q4 by our math. Does that jump rely on higher-margin European pouch mix, $8.0 million of assumed government grant credits, or tariff refunds?

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐐𝟑 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐔𝐤𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞?
Shipments to Ukraine-based customers represented 31% of Q2 sales. With U. S. revenue more than doubling to $12.2 million in Q3, how much did Ukraine concentration decline in the quarterly filing's geographic table?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐎𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Contracted backlog in the 10-Q sat at $36.5 million in June, down from $53.3 million in Q3 2025. Did multi-quarter customer orders rebuild the order book, or does Q4 still depend on in-quarter orders?

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖?
The $75 million Department of War contract funds the conversion of an existing U. S. battery line for up to 12 million cells a year in 2028. Is this facility run by Nanotech Energy or a new partner?

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐛 𝐭𝐨 $𝟒𝟓.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Unpaid customer bills now exceed an entire quarter's revenue at 117% of Q3 sales, and two customers owed 54% of the balance in June. Have collections accelerated in October, or have payment terms lengthened?
